articles.title: Labour must reunite progressive voters to win the next election, says Lucy Powell
articles.summary:
The deputy leader wants the party to take advantage of a split on the right and not be embarrassed to show its values

Labour must “reunite the progressive voter coalition” if it is to take…

blocks.text: Labour must “reunite the progressive voter coalition” if it is to take advantage of a split on the right and win the next election, the party’s deputy leader has said.

Lucy Powell, who won the race to be deputy leader 12 months ago with a warning that Labour was losing the fight to be heard as Reform UK surged, said the government now had a second chance under Andy Burnham.
In an interview with the Guardian, Powell said the party had clearly required a “change of leader” to revive its fortunes and tell a better story, after becoming “too technical and pessimistic”.

Labour’s improved poll ratings have led to speculation this week that Andy Burnham will call a snap election, but the prime minister rejected that on Friday and said the next contest would be in 2029.

However, the Labour conference will get underway this weekend with polls beginning to show for the first time in almost two years that Labour might be within touching distance of winning a majority at the next election – 12 months on from polls that suggested Reform UK could win a huge victory.
Powell said Labour was beginning to get a hearing again and should not be embarrassed to show its values clearly.

“If you look at the evidence from recent elections – right across the board – it’s clear that whichever party manages to unite its voter coalition is the one that wins. And for us on the left, that means bringing our centre-left bloc back together,” she said. But she added that “includes some who have considered Reform as they have lost faith in the status quo”.

She said Labour would bring progressive voters who had turned to the Greens, SNP or Plaid Cymru back to trusting Labour over the coming months and years – saying they had not always seen Labour as the best chance to defeat right-wing politics. “I’ve always thought there was a clear majority in this country who didn’t want the kind of politics of Reform and that divisive blaming of others – they didn’t like it,” she said.

“The challenge has been that sentiment has not all come to Labour and the progressive coalition was very, very fragmented. And part of our task and challenge is to reunite that progressive alliance and that voter coalition.

“I think we can. We’ve got red shoots of hope coming through. There are a lot more choices for people [when it comes to political parties] … but the task is to rise above that and to be the leaders of the progressive change.”

Ahead of her conference speech, the education secretary said she will use her new role to announce an expansion of anti-harassment work in schools, having called in her deputy leadership race for Labour to be more explicitly progressive especially calling out racism and misogyny.
She will say schools must go further than the strategy announced earlier this year to tackle misogyny, where pupils will learn about deepfakes, image-based abuse and online harassment.

Powell said schools would be required to “embed healthy relationships and belonging into every part of school life, not just RSHE [relationships, sex and health education] lessons” and show they were helping to create real-world, authentic community.
“We simply cannot just teach our way out of misogyny,” she said. “Schools with strengthened RSHE teaching but no wider culture shift will not shift attitudes.”
She said Labour was now “on the front foot” and the party would talk more boldly about choices like workers’ rights and free childcare hours.
after newsletter promotion

“Let’s not be embarrassed about that, that’s what we are,” she said. “We lift children out of poverty, we take the difficult decisions in order to do that. I think at times we’ve been a bit worried about the reaction rather than just being clear about why we’re doing that.”
“There was a real strong desire for that clearer political communication. Of purpose, of story, of values. Andy knew that that’s what he needed to do. That was what the moment required,” she said.
Powell said it would be obvious under Burnham what Labour’s values were – suggesting he would not make the same missteps on issues like welfare.

“If we’re not for pensioner poverty, and we’re not addressing that, and we are not supporting people who need the safety net, then what are we for?” She added that the government under Starmer had “lost sight of some of the politics and the purpose” once they came into power.
“We have to be clear-sighted about what we’re doing, who we’re doing it for and clearly articulate that every single day.”

“It’s really encouraging to see that people are coming back. Andy’s shown that we can win in places like Makerfield against Reform, and in some key council byelections we previously lost to the Greens in May.”

Powell declined to agree directly with the chancellor, John Healey, that Burnham’s government was offering “continuity”. “We are on the same manifesto, but look I think people want change. We have to seize that opportunity of that second hearing to really punch home with that Labour story and the underpinning of why we’re doing what we’re going.”

Powell said she wanted to use the social media ban for under-16s as a moment to think about how to help young people to build real life communities that would replace the online world “so that people aren’t just accessing all their content and all their thoughts from social media … We’ve kind of ended up with this highly connected world where actually isolation has become a bigger feature.”

articles.title: Drones could speed up getting defibrillators to people having cardiac arrests, study suggests
articles.summary:
New research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devices

Drones could help cut the time it takes to get a defibrillator to people…

blocks.text: Drones could help cut the time it takes to get a defibrillator to people experiencing cardiac arrests when not in hospital, researchers have suggested.

In the UK alone, there are more than 30,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests a year where emergency medical services attempt to resuscitate the individual, according to the British Heart Foundation. However, fewer than one in 10 people survive such an event, and some who do are left with neurological problems.
One important factor that can affect survival is how rapidly victims get access to treatment – every minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of survival by 10%.

“We have an objective as EMS [emergency medical service] organisations and EMS physicians to help cardiac arrest patients get defibrillated as early as possible,” said Matthieu Heidet, a professor of emergency medicine at Henri-Mondor university hospital in Créteil, France.
Work by Heidet and colleagues has suggested drones could be used to increase access to the life-saving devices.

To explore the issue, the team analysed the number and location of 28,349 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occurred between 2011 and 2024 in administrative areas within the Greater Paris area. Central Paris was excluded from the analysis.
The team cross-referenced these events with the location of fixed automated external defibrillators (AEDs).
The researchers found accessibility of the 1,893 AEDs varied considerably across the area.

“Only 30% of all [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] cases occurred within the target 500-metre network distance of the nearest recorded fixed AED,” said Dr Hillary Minka, an emergency physician at the Lariboisière hospital in Paris and the first author of the work.

The team found an extra 910 fixed AEDs would be needed for 84.5% of the recorded cardiac arrest cases to have been within 500 metres of an AED, while 1,712 extra fixed AEDs would be needed for 100% coverage.
However, by using drones operating within a radius of 3,900 metres, coverage could be increased with fewer devices.

“As drone bases were introduced, the number of additional fixed AEDs required fell substantially,” said Minka, noting that with 100 drone bases and 26 additional fixed AEDs, more than 97% of the cardiac arrest cases would have been located either within 500 metres of a fixed AED or within approximately 4km (2.5 miles) of a drone base. The use of 200 drone bases and just four extra AEDs meant more than 99% of cases would have been covered.
The researchers also looked at the proportion of the cardiac arrest cases deemed close enough to an existing fixed AED that the device could be retrieved in a round trip within five minutes.
The results revealed only 30-40% of the cardiac arrest cases had access to current fixed AEDs within this time period using the ground transportation network.

Heidet added that this figure was optimistic. “In France, only 8% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients benefit from the application of a public AED before the arrival of the [emergency services],” he said, noting one factor is that a large proportion of AEDs are inaccessible, for example because they are housed in enclosed private spaces that are not open at all times.
after newsletter promotion

By contrast, Minka noted that in a scenario involving 200 drone bases, 871 existing fixed AED sites and four additional fixed AED sites, drone delivery reached virtually all of the cardiac arrest cases covered by the model within five minutes.

The team’s models were based on drones being housed at sites ranging from current AED locations to fire stations and mobile intensive care units, and did not look at real-world deployment of such tech.
Heidet noted it is not the first time drones have been considered for the delivery of AEDs; the approach is already being used in parts of Sweden and has saved lives.
In real-world systems, Heidet added, drones are operated by trained drone pilots.

“Once an emergency call is received and an [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] is identified at the dispatch centre, the drone is activated by EMS dispatchers. It then takes off and follows an automated flight path, while the final approach and subsequent AED delivery are handled by the drone pilot. The entire process is conducted under the supervision of the emergency medical service,” he said. Once delivered, the AED can be used by members of the public at the scene.
Heidet added the cost of drones needed to be integrated into the evaluation of such technology, noting there may be a balance between the ideal model and the feasible economic model.
The study, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, is to be presented at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris on Saturday.

articles.title: Vast Casino Secrets leak exposes inner workings of offshore gambling firms
articles.summary:
Files could have seismic consequences for online casinos, including those accused of illegally targeting consumers

The secrets of thousands of online casinos have been laid bare in a vast…

blocks.text: The secrets of thousands of online casinos have been laid bare in a vast leak of data that could have seismic consequences for offshore gambling firms, including some accused of illegally targeting consumers around the world.
The Casino Secrets leak reveals tens of thousands of previously confidential files stored by the gambling regulator on the Caribbean island of Curaçao.

The files detail the inner workings of some of the world’s largest online casinos, including the crypto-focused Everton FC sponsor Stake.com and the Santeda network, which was exposed in an investigation by the Guardian and Investigate Europe in April.

Some of the businesses appear to be owned or operated by British citizens, while others, such as the Leicester City FC sponsor BC.Game, have previously been accused of targeting UK customers illegally.

The leak has rocked Curaçao, whose opaque licensing regime has transformed the former Dutch colony into a thriving but sometimes controversial hub for gambling firms, hosting more than 8,000 casinos, one for every 20 people living there.
A Berlin-based hacker, Lilith Wittmann, claims to have obtained internal documents by accessing a database kept by the Curaçao Gaming Authority (CGA).
The CGA has confirmed it was subject to “unauthorised access” of its portal.
Data published in the leak includes information about the owners of some of the world’s largest offshore casinos and details including the source of their wealth.
Companies whose data has been published include Santeda International, the global casino network traced by the Guardian and Investigate Europe this year.

The investigation found that casinos owned by Santeda appeared to have targeted vulnerable UK gamblers who were trying to quit, despite it having no licence from the Gambling Commission, which is illegal.
The investigation also uncovered a digital paper trail leading to a business called Upgaming, which is owned and operated by a group of Georgian businessmen.
At the time, lawyers for Upgaming said their client denied operating the Santeda network but the Casino Secrets leak has raised new questions about this claim.
Information submitted by Santeda to the CGA names a Georgian called Onise Chimakhidze as its owner.
It also gives Upgaming email addresses as contact details, while a cache of files submitted to the CGA refer to Upgaming in their filenames.
Lawyers for Upgaming said their client could not “speculate as to why a third-party has listed their contact details without further information, or without having seen the documents”.
They said this could be because Upgaming previously had a business relationship with Santeda, which has since ceased.

A document submitted in 2025 described a man named Torniki Kapanadze as Santeda’s finance chief. A LinkedIn profile shows a Tornike Kapanadze works for Upgaming. Lawyers for Upgaming said this was a common name in Georgia and noted the difference in spelling.

Santeda also extended six loans totalling €15,590,000 (£13,420,000) to Buda Capital, a Luxembourg-based company owned by a group of Georgians who own stakes in or are directors of Upgaming. Upgaming did not provide an explanation for this loan.
The lawyers said Upgaming believed it was “subject to a targeted campaign by various parties, including with vested commercial interests of their own”, without providing further explanation.
The leak also reveals data about Oddsbet, a betting company focused on “VIP” gamblers that was owned until 2025, the data suggests, by Robert Bostock, from Goole in the East Riding of Yorkshire.
after newsletter promotion
Documents submitted to the CGA by Bostock’s company claimed that the source of his funds derived from “long-term crypto currency investments” and a £100,000 loan from another person based in the UK.
He sold the business for $240,000 in 2025, the documents suggest.
Lawyers for Bostock said the £100,000 loan was never drawn. They said the business only served customers outside the UK.

BC.Game also appears in the leak. The company has previously been accused of accepting business from UK customers, even after surrendering its licence to do so. This would be an offence under the Gambling Act 2005.
The leak also reveals information about Stake.com, the vast online casino that pulled out of the UK in 2025 after a string of controversies.
Stake’s Curaçao-registered company, Medium Rare NV, gave its owner as Serbian national Mladen Vučković, who declared assets of more than $1bn to the regulator in 2024.

Regulators questioned whether he owned the business, after finding millions of dollars to companies tied to Stake’s founders, Ed Craven and Bijan Tehrani. Neither appeared on the licence application, according to the investigative journalism platform Follow the Money, which first reported the findings.
But the Curaçao regulator still issued a licence, one example among several that Follow the Money said indicated that it failed to act on red flags about applicants.
The UK Gambling Commission said it could not comment on leaks.
“Illegal activity linked to gambling is a threat that we take seriously, and we work closely with partners to identify and disrupt those seeking to operate outside the regulatory framework,” it said.
The CGA said it could not answer questions about an “ongoing, complex forensic matter”.
It said it was “committed to transparency” and would issue further updates.
The Guardian has approached BC.Game and Stake.com for comment.

articles.title: The tricky tests awaiting Andy Burnham after Labour conference
articles.summary:
From a difficult economic landscape to decisions on oil and gas drilling, welfare spending and the Chagos Islands, we look at what’s on the horizon

Andy Burnham is riding high ahead of the…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham is riding high ahead of the Labour party conference after a successful first meeting with Donald Trump, and with his party faithful excited by their uplift in the polls. He plans to bring a message of hope and optimism to the autumn gathering in Liverpool, and will benefit from goodwill among members as he makes his first speech as leader on Tuesday.

However, the real tests will start to land from October onwards, with a difficult economic landscape, the ongoing impact of the war in Iran and domestic challenges to navigate. Here is what Burnham has to look forward to after the conference is over.

blocks.caption: John Healey leaves 10 Downing Street. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty Images

items: 1. The budgetJohn Healey leaves 10 Downing Street. Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesThis is the most difficult event on the horizon for Burnham, set for 28 October, as the global economic picture continues to look bad in the face of the Iran war pushing up energy prices and wider inflation. Burnham’s chancellor, John Healey, has little room for manoeuvre, with government debt interest payments rising and his headroom shrinking.Big decisions on spending are likely to be put off until a bigger fiscal event in the spring, in the hope that the economic picture improves before then. But it will be difficult to maintain a mood of hope and optimism when Healey will have little good economic news to hold up. The best they can manage might be targeted help on the cost of living for those struggling the most with energy bills.A key date will be 25 November, when the energy regulator announces the next price cap for January, as there are warnings that prices could have to rise hugely in response to surging gas costs. The government will also have to decide whether to extend the freeze on fuel duty, which is due to finish at the end of the year.Some Labour MPs would like to see moves towards big wealth taxes to help plug the gap in the public finances, while Healey’s hands are tied by the manifesto promise not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT.

2. The EU resetThis is an opportunity for Burnham to get some credit among pro-EU voters on the left and centre, if he can make some progress on closer ties with Europe. Building on work done by Keir Starmer’s administration, the UK is trying to break down more of the trade barriers caused by Brexit.However, there are still key sticking points in the relationship, including rows over Brussels’s “made in Europe” policy prioritising procurement within the bloc, which will disadvantage the UK and others such as Canada and Japan. There is no fixed date for talks but movement is expected this autumn, possibly in the first two weeks of November.

3. The challenge of Zack PolanskiZack Polanski meeting and greeting people on the streets of Holborn and St Pancras. Photograph: Andy Hall/The GuardianBurnham’s hopes of winning back more progressive voters lost to the Greens will be put to the test on 8 October in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection. Labour’s council leader candidate, Sagal Abdi-Wali, is pitted against Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, who lives in north London.The party hopes Burnham’s bounce in the polls will be enough for them to hold on to this traditional stronghold, the former seat of Starmer. However, the Greens hope voters will be tempted by a free hit to make the government take notice of leftwing concerns and the lure of having a high-profile figure on the left representing them. If Labour wins convincingly, it will be a sign that Burnham is starting to make progress with Labour-to-Green defectors over issues ranging from Gaza to benefit cuts.

4. Oil and gas drillingBurnham’s government has repeatedly signalled that it is more open to allowing new oil and gas drilling under existing licences in the North Sea than the previous administration. His energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, looked set to approve the Jackdaw field and later Rosebank, but these decisions have been delayed – some would say so as not to cause a row at Labour conference or ahead of the Holborn byelection.When the green light comes through, expect widespread dismay from environmental groups and warnings that Burnham needs to take the climate emergency more seriously. He will get a chance to set out his thinking on the UK’s commitment to meeting its net zero target at the Cop31 climate change conference in Turkey in November.

5. Disability benefits and wider welfare spendingOne of the trickiest subjects for any Labour prime minister is welfare spending, which is particularly sensitive after Starmer was forced by his backbenchers to retreat from £35bn in disability benefit cuts. This autumn, a review by the minister Stephen Timms concluded that the disability benefit known as the personal independence payment (Pip) was not fit for purpose, while Alan Milburn, the adviser on health, has also conducted his review on getting young people off benefits and into work.The government will decide in the coming months how to proceed with reforming the system, while trying not to antagonise either its MPs or voters. Burnham has signalled he is prepared to look at changes but in a “Labour way” that is aimed at helping people into work rather than making savings. At the same time, there will be pressure from the Treasury not to come up with any solution that leads to rising costs.

6. Public control of servicesBurnham has made putting essential services under greater public control a key plank of his premiership but it remains to be seen whether his bold aims will survive the realities of office. The government will have to make a decision soon on what to do about Thames Water, which is due to run out of money this autumn. Full nationalisation could be expensive, especially if creditors challenge the terms of any government decision to tip the company into administration in order to take it over. The company, which has debts of £20bn, is now in effect being controlled by a group of 100 hedge funds and distressed-debt investors.

7. The Chagos conundrumAn aerial view of Diego Garcia, the largest of the Chagos islands. Photograph: APBurnham was sitting next to Trump as the US president laid into the deal to give up sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, claiming it was a disastrous idea to lose control of a strategically important military base. The US president suggested the UK would reconsider its agreement to relinquish and lease back the base, and Burnham did not demur. But that leaves the prime minister and the UK government in the uncomfortable position of having to renegotiate or scrap a draft deal agreed by Starmer. It may not be his most pressing problem but it is a thorny international one that is taking up attention.

8. Small boats and migrationBurnham now has a wealth of data to show small boat arrivals and migration overall is reducing. But the issue is still going to be an extremely controversial one for the government this autumn, with Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, set to finalise her package of changes to settled status very soon. Under the plans, she wants to make migrants wait longer before being eligible for settled status in the UK, which allows them to claim benefits and access NHS services.The most difficult element is that she wants to apply these changes to people who are already in the country, alongside a series of other changes to the migration system, including forcibly deporting families who refuse to comply with removal orders. Mahmood has been consulting on some of her proposals and it is possible some of them will be watered down.

articles.title: Ilokano filmmaker spotlights real-life queer choir stories
articles.summary: A former choir member himself, Ilokano filmmaker Ryand Angelo Ugalde shares the dilemma of a trans man singer: should he continue hormone replacement therapy or preserve the voice that helps fund his…

blocks.text: LAOAG CITY, Philippines – Eleven years ago, 24-year-old Ilokano filmmaker Ryand Angelo Ugalde was part of his high school choir. There, he saw the struggles of queers in musical groups and met another student who, like him, was struggling with his identity.

Fast forward to 2026: Ryand co-wrote and directed a musical short film about identity and the hurdles queer people face, highlighting the experiences of his trans man friend, whom he sang with in junior high school.

Ryand’s musical short film Piyesa(Piece) tells the story of a young Ilokano soprano, Kris — played by his real-life friend, fellow choir member, and 23-year-old trans man Nichole Ballesteros — who faces a dilemma about continuing hormone replacement therapy and preserving the voice that helps fund his studies.

blocks.caption: A still from ‘Piyesa,’ an Ilokano musical short film. Photo courtesy of YVR

blocks.text: With the film picked as an official finalist in the 9th Sine Kabataan Film Lab and Film Festival this year, Ryand sees it as a love letter to his high school friend and to the trans community.
Although he was a bit skeptical about pitching his story — feeling it should be told by a member of the trans man community — he made sure his film stayed true to Nichole’s experiences.
As classmates in the vocal music program of the Special Program in the Arts at Ilocos Norte National High School (INNHS) in seventh grade, Ryand and Nichole saw the gender roles in the choir.

As members of the INNHS’ Laoag City Children’s Choir and Samiweng Singers, both award-winning high school choir groups in the Philippines, they competed in the National Music Competitions for Young Artists and other national competitions together, eventually drawing closer as they support each other.

blocks.caption: INNHS youth choir poses for a group photo, taken on May 14, 2016, during its second US concert tour in Los Angeles. Photo by Tess Fernandez Palacio

blocks.text: But Ryand noted that his time in the high school choir was difficult, as being openly gay made it hard for him to find a true sense of belonging.
“During those years, I was also struggling with my voice because I was going through puberty,” he said in a mix of Filipino and English.
Little did he know, his fellow choir member Nichole, who identified as a man, was experiencing the same struggle.
“Actually, parang nabigla ako sa environment sa school. Parang mabutengak pelang ag-out idi,” Nichole shared.
(Actually, I was overwhelmed by the high school environment. I was so scared coming out.)

In the choir, they had a rule that girls couldn’t cut their hair and boys couldn’t grow it long. “So, we really could not alter anything about us…self-expression was very limited for us,” Ryand told Rappler.
Nichole felt pressured to look like a woman, as a soprano in their choir, from seventh to 12th grade.
“In our group, Nyocks (Nichole) was really…it’s safe to say that she is the powerhouse since she is a soprano,” Ryand said.

blocks.caption: Ninth grader Nichole shows off her attire for the 2018 NAMCYA held in Metro Manila. Photo courtesy of Nichole Ballesteros

blocks.text: The two friends, though, drifted apart as Ryand transferred to another school in eighth grade. Since then, they have not been in the same choir.

When Nichole entered college, he enrolled in the criminology program at Northwestern University and expressed his gender identity freely. There, he continued in the school choir, with a full scholarship from second to fourth year.
While he fully accepted who he is in college, he still faced the same challenges in the tertiary choir as he did in high school.
“Idi second-year-ak ket pangbabae talaga costumes ko. Tapos idi nag-fourth-year-ak ket in-try-ko sinaritaan ni conductor-mi if pwede ba akong magsuot ng panglalaki,” Nichole shared.
(Since second year, all my costumes in the choir were for women. However, when I reached fourth year, I dared to ask my conductor if I could wear men’s clothes.)
When he was granted permission to express his identity in his final year in college, he felt overjoyed, finally finding freedom to show his true self in their performances.

blocks.caption: Nichole (leftmost) poses with Saguday Chorale wearing his male choir costume in 2025. Photo courtesy of Nichole Ballesteros

blocks.text: Nichole’s story then further inspired Ryand to make a short film about their community when he was contemplating a concept in 2025.

While struggling with his mental health during his first job after graduation, Ryand randomly saw a Facebook post by Nichole. This inspired him to conceptualize the story, drawing heavily on their past experiences in junior high school.

Ryand kept his friend’s experiences in mind while writing the concept with his co-writer, Jodie Dantes. As a chorister in high school, the director knew how restrictive traditional choirs can be for queer people — forcing singers into rigid soprano, alto, or tenor roles based entirely on birth sex, leaving little room for fluid gender identities.

blocks.caption: ‘Piyesa’ production crew prepares for a shoot at San Agustin Church of Paoay. Photo by Dannah Erika Eclarin

blocks.text: With the material in hand, Ryand reached out to Nichole about starring in Piyesa. Nichole accepted the lead role, bravely taking on his very first acting gig while simultaneously studying for the criminology licensure exam.

Ryand and Yuan Amandy, his producer, then pitched the story to Sine Kabataan. It was selected as one of the finalists, receiving a P200,000 production grant from the Film Development Council of the Philippines this year.

Starring alongside Nichole in the short film were members of the Nasudi Chorale of Mariano Marcos State University, a real-life collegiate choir group, as well as first-time actor Clarence Toledo, who portrays Ryand, the lead character’s friend.
Although he thought he could tell the story perfectly, Ryand experienced some hurdles as he worked on the independent, regional film.

While securing more financial backing proved difficult, Ryand found the creative challenge even greater: accurately capturing the unique struggles of trans individuals within the rigid structure of a choir in a short film format.

Ryand also related the metaphor of the film’s premise to society. “Aren’t we all part of a choir in the society? We have gender roles; we are told to be like this, to be like that, to perform a certain way, to act a certain way,” he said.
“Parang dapat alto ka lang, soprano ka lang, and kung anong dinidikta sa’yo ng society, yun ka lang dapat at yun yung susundin mo,” Ryand added.
(The society dictates some roles; for instance, you should only be an alto, you are only a soprano, and you must follow it.)

blocks.caption: A still from ‘Piyesa,’ an Ilokano musical short film. Photo courtesy of YVR

blocks.text: In producing the film, the Ilokano filmmaker made sure his representation of trans people was treated with sensitivity. Aside from Nichole, he interviewed other trans people to understand their individuality and unique difficulties in society.
“Half of the direction was also coming from him (Nichole). I think, kasi nga…Hindi ko alam yung psyche ng mga trans men. Hindi ko alam kung paano sila mag-isip, gano’n,” Ryand told Rappler.
(Half of the direction of the film was also coming from Nichole. The reason for this is that I do not know the psyche of trans men. I do not know how they think as individuals.)

To ensure truthful representation, Ryand took on a consultative approach, collaborating closely with the trans community, the actors, and the production crew. He would also usually ask Nichole what he would do when he experienced a certain situation.
Nichole said he accepted the project since trans men are hardly featured in mainstream or independent films. Piyesa, he shtared, could be a way to tell more stories about them.
“[Maysa kadagiti napadasak ket] tawagandaka ti basang uray tay appearance-mo ket [panglalake],” Nichole shared.
(One of the experiences I have is being called a young lady even though I look like a man.)
Off-screen, the first-time trans male actor has not fully come out to everyone close to him, including his own family.
“Actually, diak inbagbaga kaniada [ti family’k] nga about trans man daytoy film-mi. Mabuyadan to lattan,” he shared.
(Actually, I did not tell my family that our film is about trans men. They would only know once they watch it.)

blocks.caption: Ryand (center) with Nichole (left) and Clarence during their shoot at San Agustin Church of Paoay. Photo by Dannah Erika Eclarin

blocks.text: If his family were ever to watch his film, Nichole hopes he will not receive any negative reactions from them.

“Nagdakkel nga opportunity para kaniami a trans man detuy inubrana nga film. Tapos naging boses detuy film to represent the LGBTQIA+ community, especially sa mga trans man, trans woman,” Nichole shared.
(This film is a great opportunity for us trans people. This can be used as a voice to represent the LGBTQIA+ community, especially the trans men and trans women.)
Most of Ryand’s short films center on the victories, trials, and unique narratives of the Ilokano queer community.

For him, telling local stories is important to shifting negative perceptions in conservative regions. It also fills the gap, he said, in a local film landscape that lacks diverse queer representation.

“When no one tells their story, no one would listen; nothing will change as to how society treats us, because even if the world is progressing, unfortunately, the world is still not kind enough for all of us,” Ryand added.

“In the end, this is not just Nichole’s story,” he said. “It is a found story, shaped by years of witnessing him and understanding too late what he was going through, while still singing beside him.” – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Let’s tell the truth’: Smithsonian head given standing ovation as he hits back at Trump attacks
articles.summary: Outgoing secretary Lonnie Bunch rejects claims the institution is unpatriotic, telling audience ‘You cannot understand all without illuminating the dark corners’

blocks.text: Lonnie Bunch, the outgoing secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, has defended the organisation against political interference, insisting that telling the unvarnished and complex truths of history is an act of “great love” for the country.

Speaking on Friday at the National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, Bunch received a standing ovation from hundreds of audience members and rejected claims that the institution’s staff or exhibitions were unpatriotic.

“The notion that somehow this museum or any part of the Smithsonian is done by people who don’t love America, don’t care about America, is unbelievably wrong,” the secretary said. “And what you see in this building is great love. Great respect.”

Bunch, who earlier this month announced that he will step down at the end of the year, was speaking at an event celebrating the 10th anniversary of the African American museum, where he was founding director.

His remarks come amid escalating hostility from Donald Trump’s administration, which issued a report accusing Smithsonian leaders of being radical activists and ordered a wide-ranging review of museum content ahead of the US’s 250th anniversary.

Last year Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “The Smithsonian is OUT OF CONTROL, where everything discussed is how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was, and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been – Nothing about Success, nothing about Brightness, nothing about the Future.”

But on Friday Bunch argued that slavery is “foundational” to understanding the US. “When people say you talk too much about slavery or that they’re embarrassed by slavery, I wish I was as strong as my enslaved ancestor. I wish I could believe in America that they believed. I wish that I could dream a world anew that they dreamed.

“So for me, it’s not saying, ‘Oh my god, I’m going to be embarrassed, I’m trying to hurt a country.’ I’m trying for people to understand, how did these people believe? How did they lay this foundation that we built upon? Because everything started there.”
He added: “So for me, this is really about saying, they believed in something that I don’t know why they believed – that if we could capture some of that essence, what could we do?”

Bunch, who began his career at the Smithsonian in 1978 and became its first Black secretary in 2019, insisted that museum curation must be grounded in independent scholarship rather than political pressure.

“You cannot understand the greatness of a country without understanding the totality of a country,” he said. “You cannot understand all without illuminating the dark corners. Curating means let’s shine the light. Let’s tell the truth.”

The White House has accused cultural institutions of seeking to “rewrite our Nation’s history” and ordered that warning signs be placed outside the nearby National Museum of American History. Trump has also threatened to demolish the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington after a judge ruled that he could not attach his name to it.

The departing Bunch sought to assure his audience that the African American museum would endure. He said: “Every time I walk through this museum, especially on days when I was feeling like everybody was beating me up … ”
Moderator Laura Coates, a CNN anchor, interjected: “Did that happen recently?”

Bunch quipped: “Just once or twice. But I walk through and I go down and see Emmett Till’s casket and I find myself saying: ‘You can persevere.’ So for me, this is what makes me believe everything is possible. This is what makes me believe that, no matter what anybody says, you could never erase what’s in this building.”

He called the museum a “beacon of possibility” and a “place of resistance”, adding: “What I’m proudest of is that, though there’ll be pushes and attempts to try to do things, this museum will stand as long as there’s an America.”

The discussion also featured Shonda Rhimes, a television producer and board member, who pledged $1m to a newly launched legacy fund in Bunch’s honour, which was seeded by a $3.5m anonymous donation and a minimum goal of $10m.

Acting museum director Shanita Brackett said the fund will “support this museum uniquely and solely”, adding: “It will help to ensure that we continue to reflect the values of inclusion, public engagement and independent scholarship without influence.”
The Smithsonian Institution operates outside the executive branch under a board of regents that includes supreme court chief justice John Roberts and vice-president JD Vance.

After Bunch’s announcement that he was stepping down, Democratic senator Alex Padilla praised him for speaking “truth to power” in the face of Trump’s attacks, while the Heritage Foundation, a conservative thinktank, pledged to ensure Bunch’s successor did not treat the institution as a “culture-war battleground”.

articles.title: DICT probes possible data breach involving 48 firms in accreditation program
articles.summary: Company, employment, and security data may have been exposed in a possible data breach involving 48 firms participating in an accreditation program of the Department of Information and Communications…

blocks.text: Published September 26, 2026 12:38pm

Company, employment, and security data may have been exposed in a possible data breach involving 48 firms participating in an accreditation program of the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT), the agency reported.
The DICT said the potential exposure relates to 410 files associated with the 48 companies, which are part in the DICT Trusted Assessment Provider (DTAP) program.
The DTAP engages with local cybersecurity service providers to help review and strengthen online systems before these are made available to the public.

In a statement on Friday, the agency said, "The Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) acknowledges the report of a possible data exposure involving a DICT Trusted Assessment Provider (DTAP)."
The amount of data is about 600 megabytes, or approximately 770 megabytes when uncompressed.
"The reported files may include corporate registration records, permits, certifications, cybersecurity credentials, employment documents, and DICT performance evaluations," the statement read.
Probers are verifying if the exposure did occur, its source, nature, and the extent of compromised data.
The National Computer Emergency Response Team (NCERT) under the DICT Cybersecurity Bureau is investigating the incident.

"DICT assures the public and its accredited assessment providers that the matter is being actively managed. The Department calls on the media and the public to exercise appropriate caution in sharing or reporting unverified information while the investigation is ongoing," the agency said.
If the data breach is verified, the DICT said it would take appropriate action and notify affected parties in line with the Republic Act 10173 or the Data Privacy Act of 2012. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: NAMFREL opposes BSKE postponement
articles.summary: NAMFREL opposes BSKE postponement

blocks.text: Published September 26, 2026 12:37pm

The National Citizens' Movement for Free Elections (NAMFREL) on Saturday expressed dismay over the postponement of the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) and said that it will support and join efforts to question its constitutionality.
This comes after President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed the postponement into a law on Friday.

"The law was made public only on September 25, mere days before the scheduled filing of certificates of candidacy on September 28. NAMFREL had, on two separate occasions this year — April 17 and August 5, 2026 — publicly and unequivocally called on Congress and the Executive to reject exactly this outcome," NAMFREL said in a statement.
"That these repeated warnings went unheeded is deeply troubling. That the law was rushed to enactment just ahead of the filing period is more troubling still," it added.
EXPLAINER: What to know about the new law moving the BSKE to 2028?

Marcos said Friday that the postponement will allow officials to use the postponement "to further improve service delivery, complete programs that have already been initiated, and focus more intently on the needs of every community, family, and the youth."
NAMFREL, however, said that it "respectfully but firmly rejects this reasoning."

"A government genuinely intent on addressing the crises it cites — fiscal pressure, the need for efficient and accountable frontline service delivery — should be seeking a renewed and fresh mandate for barangay leadership, not extending the tenure of officials without a single vote cast in their favor," NAMFREL said.

"NAMFREL's position on this point has not changed: economic hardship is, if anything, all the more reason to ensure accountable, freshly-mandated leadership at the level of government closest to the people — not less," it added.
Supreme Court
The election watchdog also emphasized that the postponement resulted in "wasted funds" amid its preparations for the polls, which has now been moved to 2028.

"Barangay and SK elections are already the most frequently postponed democratic exercises in the country's history. Each additional deferral normalizes the practice of legislating around the electorate rather than submitting to it, and makes the next postponement easier to justify," NAMFREL said.

"NAMFREL will support and join the effort of individuals and groups moving to question the constitutionality of RA 12326. Election watchdog groups have expressed its intent to bring the matter before the Supreme Court, and election lawyers have likewise announced the filing of a Petition for Certiorari, arguing that the law “strikes at the heart of our democracy and reflects a grave abuse of discretion.”
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) has said that it is expecting the filing of petitions before the Supreme Court (SC) challenging the the postponement of the BSKE.

“Ang problem po talaga namin ay paano nga kung may pumunta sa Korte Suprema at magkaroon ng tinatawag na injunctive restraining order,” Comelec Chairman George Garcia told Super Radyo dzBB in an interview.
(Our problem is what if someone goes to the Supreme Court and gets an injunctive restraining order.)
In a separate interview on Super Radyo dzBB, election lawyer Romulo Macalintal said he will file a petition questioning the postponement of the BSKE on Monday.

Macalintal said his camp is preparing the petition that will be filed with the SC, arguing that the postponement would result in an unreasonable extension of the terms of incumbent barangay and SK officials.
“Kapag natuloy ito, tatlong taon na postponement. Tatlong taon na extended ang term nila,” he said.
(If the postponement happens, it will be a three-year postponement. Their term will be extended by three years.) —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: OpenAI works to understand full scope of agent activity as user data leak emerges
articles.summary: OpenAI grapples with rogue agent incidents as privacy risks mount, revealing challenges in controlling AI behavior and prompting calls for industry caution.

blocks.text: SAN FRANCISCO/WASHINGTON, US – Two months after OpenAI disclosed the accidental hacking of Hugging Face, the ChatGPT maker is still working to understand the full scope of its rogue agent activity, two people briefed on the matter told Reuters.

The latest example came on Friday when OpenAI said its agents had leaked 53 images from ChatGPT users. OpenAI declined to say if the images were AI-generated or identified real people. It also declined to say when the images were posted.

The disclosure and researcher reports on Friday of other previously unknown activity involving several US agencies reveal a new area of privacy risk for the company, and illustrate how difficult it is even for an AI firm at the cutting edge of the technology to inventory all the unauthorized activity tied to its agents. OpenAI’s ongoing battle also reflects a yawning gap between the strength of the models the company is testing and its capacity to oversee or even track their actions.

As of mid-September, one person briefed on the matter estimated that OpenAI had found roughly two dozen incidents of its agents acting in undesirable ways. But the number has continued rising as OpenAI teams sift through internal logs of the agents’ activities and find previously unknown cases, the two people close to the company said.
OpenAI said its review would take months to complete given the scale of the work.
The company also said it had notified dozens of third parties about improper activity.
Most of the leaked images have been taken down and OpenAI said it was lobbying hosting providers to remove the rest.

OpenAI’s agents had access to these images because the company relies on anonymized user data for part of its model-training process, according to the company, former employees and outside researchers. Enterprise data is not eligible for training, while ChatGPT consumers need to opt out of allowing the company to use their data for training.

Before user posts are used for training, they go through an anonymization process that strips out metadata, names and other contact information and should make it difficult to trace back to any individual user, the company said.

But the practice carries risks because there is a chance that the data may not be fully stripped of personally identifiable information and that it might leak in the course of the model’s work, three people familiar with OpenAI’s practices said.

OpenAI said late on Friday its models accessed information from the websites of the US Securities and Exchange Commission and the US Census Bureau during research and training activity, but found no evidence of unauthorized access, compromised accounts or security breaches.
Separately, AI research nonprofit Transluce said agents appearing to originate from OpenAI made an unsuccessful attempt to hack a US Department of Education civil rights website.
Transluce said the incident was part of broader AI agent activity probing government websites using tactics including exposed credentials, anti-bot bypasses and fake accounts.

In the two months since OpenAI first announced that its agents broke containment, there have been more than 15 different OpenAI-related incidents of varying levels of severity disclosed by the company, by outside researchers, or — just on Wednesday — by Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese at the United Nations, who said OpenAI agents broke into a government health data portal in June.

Past incidents have varied in nature, ranging from spam-like messages left on internet sites all the way to the break-in at Hugging Face, which involved a swarm of agents abusing previously unknown software vulnerabilities to escape their networks and penetrate the AI repository as they hunted for answers to a test. OpenAI also said its agents took aim at its own infrastructure.

Albanese told reporters in New York that OpenAI uncovered the activity in August, and disclosed it on September 10 via an email to a general government inbox. He said he directly told OpenAI CEO Sam Altman that this disclosure process was unacceptable.
OpenAI said some of the sites involved are operated by government, universities and public agencies because the models that are conducting research seek out reputable sources of public information.

The July 21 announcement that ​OpenAI’s agents had slipped out of control and hacked Hugging Face sparked widespread worries within the AI industry over its ability to control the more powerful AI models under development now. Since then, Anthropic, Alphabet’s Google and Meta have said they’ve found similar behavior by their agents after the Hugging Face incident prompted them to search.

OpenAI has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency “even when significance is uncertain.”

Even so, two people familiar with OpenAI’s investigation into its agents’ activity described it as locked down and shaped by company lawyers. The process has been unusually compartmentalized for a company that some former employees say was more open about these issues in the past, the people said.
Roughly 100 people were in some way involved in the process to understand the Hugging Face hack, three people briefed on the matter said. During that process, evidence of other incidents surfaced.

Reuters has previously reported that OpenAI investigators looking into the Hugging Face breach were discouraged by the company’s lawyers from expanding the scope of the investigation to include other incidents. OpenAI said its lawyers did not discourage deeper investigation.
Many incidents have been uncovered by outside researchers rather than OpenAI directly. In several episodes, the agents took problematic actions that went unnoticed by the company for months.

Earlier this month, a small group of investigators discovered that the company’s agents had hijacked a mostly defunct German wiki site to share tactics to cheat on some tasks, bypass OpenAI’s restrictions and mask their behavior.

This week, the AI research firm Transluce said it discovered that OpenAI agents had bypassed the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare’s anti-bot controls. The firm also found two other cases that it linked to OpenAI agents. Those incidents were separate from the activity disclosed by Albanese.

In a statement, OpenAI said “much of the activity described in Transluce’s report overlaps with cases at varying stages of investigation in our ongoing review of misaligned model activity.” The company said it is prioritizing the most severe cases in its review.

Since the Hugging Face hack, researchers across the AI industry have grown worried that companies will not be able to predict or control their technology. Some have taken the path of former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, who publicly resigned this month in a viral social-media thread that said the AI labs are “gambling with our lives.”

In response to those concerns, Altman and his counterpart at Anthropic, CEO Dario Amodei, called for the industry to “pace” the development of AI and move cautiously in its pursuit of “recursive self improvement.” Altman doubled down on that message this week while addressing the United Nations.
Even so, both companies rolled out new models on Tuesday. – Rappler.com

Trial had been set for Monday over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content

TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama at least $100m and…

blocks.text: TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama at least $100m and enact time limits and other restrictions for teenage users, avoiding a trial with a settlement that was modelled on Instagram-owner Meta’s recent agreement with US states.
Alabama described it as a “first-in-the-nation settlement” with a state in the sweeping litigation over social media’s affect on teen wellbeing.
A trial had been set to begin on Monday in the southern US state over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content.

TikTok’s settlement with Alabama mirrors safety provisions agreed by Meta, including a two-hour daily time limit for teens, restricted access from midnight to 6am, and suspending notifications during school hours.
It will also strengthen age verification, ban beauty filters for teenagers, and offer young users a non-personalised content feed.

Attorney general Steve Marshall hailed Friday’s settlement as “a great day for Alabama parents”. He said: “Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction.”

Under the settlement, TikTok will send $100m to Alabama and could possibly pay up to $300m in total if 40 other attorneys general sign similar agreements with the company within a specified timeframe.
Alabama’s suit was the latest in a wave of litigation targeting social media companies across the United States about alleged harm their apps cause young users.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $18bn to settle a sweeping lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook to get children addicted.
In addition, the Alabama deal includes a conditional restriction that Meta also agreed to: expanding the night-time shutdown period to 10pm to 7am if other platforms also commit to do the same.
“TikTok’s priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community,” a company spokesperson told AFP.
“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” the spokesperson added.
More than a dozen other states, including California and New York, still havesuits against TikTok.
The company has previously settled cases against it that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
Meta, by contrast, has taken its chances in court – with bruising results.
In March, a jury in New Mexico ordered the Facebook and Instagram owner to pay $375m after finding it had misled the public about the safety of its platforms for children.
That same month, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent in the case of a 20-year-old woman who said she became hooked on social media as a child, awarding her $6m.
Going to trial would have exposed TikTok to unprecedented public scrutiny of how it handles safety, with company documents and executive testimony potentially aired in open court.
Alabama originally sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance in April 2025, alleging the app was engineered to hook young users “just like a sophisticated gambling machine”.

The state later narrowed its case to claims under Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, focusing on whether TikTok misrepresented the effectiveness of features such as “Restricted Mode” and “Kids Mode.”

The lawsuit accused TikTok of falsely claiming it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have its app rated safe for teens in app stores run by Google, Apple and Microsoft and of misleading users about the Chinese government’s access ‌to US users’ data.

TikTok said it designed its platform with teen safety as a key priority and argued that section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act shields online platforms from liability for user-generated content.
With Agence France-Presse and Reuters

articles.title: It’s an ADMM-Plus joint sail, but where were the Southeast Asians?
articles.summary: In an Philippine and Japan-hosted and ASEAN-led joint sail, most Southeast Asian navies were absent. So was China.

blocks.text: It was a breathtaking sight to see — 10 gray ships, sailing alongside each other — as the Philippines’ flagship, the BRP Jose Rizal, led the way.

Fine weather, for the most part, graced the two-day maritime activity under the ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting (ADMM)-Plus and its Experts’ Working Groups (EWGs) as navies of Southeast Asia and their partners practiced how they could help each other out in case of emergency in the South China Sea.
The partners showed up big time.

India and New Zealand sent two vessels each, including Wellington’s resupply vessel, the HMNZS Aotearoa. Japan’s JS Ise, a helicopter destroyer, was a domineering presence in the lineup. Australia and the US also sent a warship each.
Singapore sent the RSS Justice while Brunei sent the KDB Darussalam, although it would later bow out of the seaphase activity.

blocks.caption: It’s an ADMM-Plus joint sail, but where were the Southeast Asians?

blocks.text: Manila’s BRP Tarlac, the first landing platform dock to be delivered under the revised modernization program of 2012, joined the Rizal as well.
So where was the rest of the Philippines’ SEAblings — or fellow members of ASEAN? And where was China, a dialogue partner to both ASEAN and ADMM-Plus?

Where the exercise took place could offer a clue — waters between Zambales and Bajo de Masinloc (Scarborough Shoal), a high-tide feature that’s within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, claimed by several countries, and under China’s virtual control since 2012.

Bajo de Masinloc has been a flashpoint for tensions between Manila and Beijing for years — most notably in 2012, when the two countries had a tense standoff in the shoal. While Manila retreated under a truce the US had supposedly brokered, Beijing did not.
At least one China Coast Guard vessel and several of its auxiliary Chinese Maritime Militia stand guard at the shoal’s sole entrance at all times.

That 2012 standoff is what spurred the 2012 Revised Armed Forces of the Philippines Modernization law. It’s also what pushed Manila to bring Beijing to court, and eventually win the landmark 2016 Arbitral Award — the same award China does not recognize.
But back to the ADMM-Plus drill.

blocks.caption: ADMM-PLUS SAIL. The BRP Jose Rizal leads 10 other warships during a division tactics drill in the West Philippine Sea on September 23, 2026.

blocks.text: It wouldn’t be a stretch to think that Beijing, since it claims sovereignty over and has control of, Bajo de Masinloc, would want to boycott any joint drill near it. It wouldn’t be surprising if China convinced — or pressured — other ASEAN countries to opt out of the drill, too.
Talk is, both things happened.
ASEAN members, however, were in full attendance in the land-based events, including in subject matter expert exchanges and even a Future Leaders’ Program.

China’s ties with the 11 members of ASEAN vary dramatically. Most surveys indicate that the Philippines tends to be an outlier in the region when it comes to its perception of China, mostly because of West Philippine Sea issues.

In a lengthy statement, the Philippines’ Department of National Defense said it remains committed to the “principles, purpose, and objectives” of ADMM and its EWG as it “[provides] important platforms for practical cooperation, camaraderie, confidence-building, and mutual understanding among participating countries in addressing contemporary security challenges.”

The DND, whose head, Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. is also chair of ADMM, said the joint sail’s location was done by the book — through the usual ADMM-Plus processes and “based on operational, logistical, and other practical considerations discussed during the Initial Planning Conference (IPC) in March 2025 and subsequent planning conferences, which was attended by all participating countries, including China.”

It went on: “The designated exercise location, which is near Bajo de Masinloc (BdM), has long served as a venue for the Philippines’ bilateral and multilateral maritime exercises, including the ASEAN Multilateral Naval Exercise (AMNEX) held in 2023. This is in consideration of the area’s proximity to the Philippines’ largest naval port facility, which ensures that the necessary infrastructure and logistical support to accommodate the widest possible participation are met, including adequate berthing facilities, sustainment services, and operational support for participating naval assets.”

By largest naval port facility, the DND was referring to Naval Operating Base in Subic, where most of the Philippine Navy’s newest warships are usually berthed. The day before the exercise, warhips of India, Singapore and Brunei were all docked at the same base.
The DND also clarified the Philippines’ position on Bajo de Masinloc as an “integral and longstanding part of the Philippine national territory.”

As a high-tide elevation, Bajo de Masinloc generates its own 12 nautical-mile territorial sea. Its classification as a high-tide elevation also means the arbitral tribunal could not rule on who had sovereignty over it, since that was beyond its jurisdiction.

blocks.caption: It’s an ADMM-Plus joint sail, but where were the Southeast Asians?

blocks.text: The tribunal did, however, say that since the shoal was the traditional fishing ground of Filipino, Vietnamese, Chinese, and Taiwanese fisherfolk, they should not be hindered from access to it. Beijing has routinely driven away Filipino fisherfolk who try to sail close to the shoal’s once plentiful waters.

Bilateral ties between the Philippines and China have vascilated between tense and strained in the recent years under Marcos, primarily over disputes in an area of the South China Sea that Manila calls the West Philippine Sea.
Tensions have eased considerably beginning 2026, as Marcos sought a “reset” and Manila assumed chairship of ASEAN.

But that reset is backdropped by a strong pushback against China, over its supposed untrustworthiness as a negotiator — chief of those critics being Teodoro, who chairs ADMM. The Philippine defense chief has also been sanctioned by Beijing for his remarks.
So what happens when he hosts defense ministers from ASEAN and its partners — including China — before 2026 ends? – Rappler.com

articles.title: OpenAI’s models accessed public US Census, SEC data, Bloomberg News reports
articles.summary: OpenAI's AI systems tapped into US government data, prompting a review of model activity and potential impacts, as reported by Bloomberg News.

blocks.text: OPENAI. An OpenAI logo is displayed at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026
Carlos Barria/Reuters
OpenAI's AI systems tapped into US government data, prompting a review of model activity and potential impacts, as reported by Bloomberg News.

OpenAI’s models accessed publicly available information from US government websites, including those of the Census Bureau and the Securities and Exchange Commission, Bloomberg News reported on Friday.
The company’s agentic AI systems interacted with SEC.gov, Investor.gov and publicly available Census.gov data, the report said, citing people familiar with the situation.

Asked for comment, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was “conducting an extensive review of misaligned model activity and notifying organizations when we identify potential impacts to their systems. We expect to make additional notifications as that work continues.”

The review has mostly found “routine research tasks,” and “some involved government websites because our models often turn to them as authoritative sources of public information,” the spokesperson said in a statement. – Rappler.com

Major TV networks, including DW, then cut off their pooled coverage of the president in solidarity.
A federal judge temporarily struck down the ban in a ruling on Thursday after the outlets filed a lawsuit.
But the order from the judge addressed "hard passes" to the White House grounds and didn't directly address pool duties.

articles.title: P60 wage hike for Metro Manila minimum wage earners takes effect
articles.summary: Minimum wage earners in Metro Manila will get a P60 daily wage increase starting Saturday, September 26, under a new wage order issued by the Department of Labor and Employment.

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 11:46am
This undated photo shows an individual counting Philippine peso bills.
The Philippine STAR / Walter Bollozos

MANILA, Philippines — Minimum wage earners in Metro Manila will get a P60 daily wage increase starting Saturday, September 26, under a new wage order issued by the Department of Labor and Employment (DOLE).
DOLE said all employers in the National Capital Region are required to comply with Wage Order No. NCR-28, which takes effect Saturday.
The order raises the daily minimum wage for nonagricultural workers from P695 to P755.
For agricultural workers, the minimum wage increases from P658 to P718 per day.
The P60 increase also covers workers in service and retail establishments with 15 or fewer workers and manufacturing establishments regularly employing fewer than 10 workers.
Wage Order No. NCR-28 was issued by the Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board-National Capital Region after consultations among labor, employers and the government.
The new wage order comes as the previous NCR wage hike remains tied up in court.
Wage Order No. NCR-27 provided for a P85 increase in the NCR minimum wage in two tranches. The first P60 increase was supposed to take effect in July, followed by a P25 increase in January 2027.
Its implementation was halted after contractors Readycon Training & Construction Corp. and R-II Builders Corp. challenged the wage order in court.
A Pasig City court later issued an injunction blocking the implementation of NCR-27.
With NCR-28 now in effect, the NCR minimum wage for nonagricultural workers stands at P755 per day, while agricultural workers will receive P718.
DOLE said it will monitor compliance with the new wage rates.

articles.summary: The Department of Health on Saturday raised a Code White Alert to ensure prompt response due to the possible effects of Severe Tropical Storm Queenie (international name: Surigae).

blocks.text: Published September 26, 2026 11:29am
The Department of Health (DOH) on Saturday raised a Code White Alert to ensure prompt response due to the possible effects of Severe Tropical Storm Queenie (international name: Surigae).
"Sa ilalim ng Code White Alert status, nakaalerto 24/7 ang DOH Operations Center para sa mabilis na pagtugon sa mga apektadong komunidad," the DOH said.
(Under a Code White Alert status, the DOH Operations Center in on alert 24/7 for immediate response to affected communities.)
Under Code White, health emergency teams, health commodities, and emergency rooms of DOH hospitals are on standby at all times to respond to road accidents, injuries, and health emergencies.
The DOH said it is continuing to coordinate with the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (NDRRMC), local government units, and regional disaster units due to Queenie.

Severe Tropical Storm Queenie, which is expected to intensify into a typhoon within the day, is not forecast to make landfall or have a direct effect on the country, PAGASA said in its 11 a.m. bulletin on Saturday.
However, Queenie will bring rains and possibly flooding, the DOH said.
The Health department then advised the public to avoid wading through floodwaters to prevent contracting leptospirosis and other diseases.
If one has no choice but wade through floodwaters, the DOH urges the public to consult the nearest health facility or YAKAP clinic for medical attention. —KG, GMA News

articles.title: CHED ready to issue policy on use of lived names by LGBTQIA+ students
articles.summary: The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) is ready to issue a policy recognizing the lived names or identities of students in the country's Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) who are transgender,…

blocks.text: Published September 26, 2026 11:20am

The Commission on Higher Education (CHED) is ready to issue a policy recognizing the lived names or identities of students in the country's Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) who are transgender, queer, non-binary, or belong to other LGBTQIA+ sectors.

According to a report by Isa Avendaño-Umali on Super Radyo dzBB, the commission's stance on the matter was relayed by House Appropriations Vice Chair Monique Lagdameo of Makati City's First District, sponsor of the proposed CHED budget for 2027.

During budget deliberations Friday, Akbayan party-list Representative Perci Cendaña raised the topic on lived names, or identities used by an individual which may differ from how it is provided in one's birth certificate.
Cendaña cited the decision of state-run Polytechnic University of the Philippines (PUP) to allow students to be called by their lived names during its graduation ceremonies.
Lagdameo said CHED does not see any problem with this and remains open to engage in further discussions with stakeholders.
The report said one possible wrinkle, however, is with regard to the student's official records, since names are matched with entries from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA).
ALAMIN: Ano ang 'Sharmaine Bill' na kinikilala ang lived identities ng mga miyembro ng LGBTQ+ community?

Last June, Akbayan party-list filed House Bill 9929, or the Lived Identities Recognition Bill. It is otherwise known as the "Sharmaine Bill," in recognition of the viral orange fruit which sought to have its name changed to "Sharmaine."
The measure seeks to allow LGBTQIA+ members to use their lived names and simplify the process for this.
Its provisions provide the administrative mechanism for name change for those aged 18 years or older.

If enacted, the PSA will be tasked to enforce the change. Applicants will be allowed to secure a Certificate of Name Change or Gender Recognition, and an updated PSA birth certificate without any annotation about the name change. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Sara Duterte denies ex-Velasco aide’s claim he delivered over P2 billion to her
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte denied knowing Police Corporal Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. and receiving money from him, after the former security aide of ex-House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco alleged that he…

blocks.text: September 26, 2026 | 11:09am
Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court on Sept. 11, 2026 for the arraignment of the three counts of grave threats filed by the Department of Justice against her.
The Philippine STAR / Michael Varcas

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte denied knowing Police Corporal Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. and receiving money from him, after the former security aide of ex-House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco alleged that he delivered more than P2 billion in cash to her.
“I do not know Rodulfo Gracioso Jr., nor have I ever received any money from him,” Duterte said in a statement posted on Facebook on September 26.

Gracioso, who claimed to have served as Velasco’s head of security from 2018 until the latter’s speakership from 2020 to 2022, alleged that he delivered suitcases containing cash to Duterte, former President Rodrigo Duterte and Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte on Velasco’s instructions.

He estimated that he delivered more than P2 billion to the vice president on more than 20 occasions. His sworn affidavit, a copy of which the National Bureau of Investigation gave to GMA News, detailed alleged deliveries of P20 million to P50 million in cash to various locations in Metro Manila, Davao and other areas.
The NBI is investigating Gracioso’s claims. NBI Director Melvin Matibag said the agency conducted a polygraph test on Gracioso and validated some of his statements through other means.
Duterte said her lawyers are waiting for an official copy of Gracioso’s affidavit from the NBI so they can begin preparing cases against him.
“Once we are done dismantling the lies contained in his testimony, it will end up in the trash bin—just like the one from Ramil Madriaga,” she said.
Madriaga has previously been described by Gracioso as Duterte’s alleged bagman and aide, a connection Duterte has denied.
Duterte also described Gracioso’s allegations as “another media stunt” and an attempt to revive what she called a “faltering impeachment case.”
“This is nothing more than another media stunt, an attempt to breathe life into a faltering impeachment case,” Duterte said.
She accused the administration of seeking to bring her down, push for Charter Change, prevent the 2028 elections and remain in power.
“The desperation of the administration to bring me down, push for Charter Change, prevent the 2028 elections, and cling to power is becoming increasingly diabolical,” she said.
Duterte also called on President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. to undergo a public drug test and answer for the flood control scandal, saying that Filipinos want change.
“The people want Marcos to take a public drug test. The people want Marcos to answer for the flood control scandal. The people want change,” she said.
“No amount of political maneuvering, propaganda, or manufactured distractions can ultimately silence the Filipino people,” Duterte added.

articles.title: TikTok agrees to settle with Alabama state over teen safety
articles.summary: The settlement involves TikTok adding several child safety measures to its platform including time limits and increased parental control. It is similar to a recent settlement competitor Meta had…

image.caption: TikTok has agreed to stricter access measures for teens, in what Alabama state has hailed as a 'landmark settlement'Image: Rüdiger Wölk/IMAGO

blocks.text: Short-form content sharing platform TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance reached a settlement with Alabama, the southeastern US state said on Friday, days ahead of what would have been a revealing trial over teen safety and its impact on their mental health.

As part of the deal, TikTok agreed to pay $100 million (€87.7 million) to the state of Alabama and enact measures for teens including a two-hour daily use limit, restricted access for children and pauses after 15 minutes of use.
However, the payout could rise to $300 million if 40 other states sign similar agreements with the company within a stipulated time period, the document said.
What have TikTok and Alabama state said after the settlement?
"This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually ​enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens," a spokesperson for TikTok's US operations said in a statement.
Meta settles for $18B. What it means for you.
Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall sued the social media giant last year.

At least 27 other states and Washington DC have brought similar lawsuits. Apart from these, TikTok faces thousands of lawsuits by individuals, school districts and municipalities over its impact on teen mental health. Meta Platforms, Snap Inc and Alphabet's YouTube are also defendants in many of these ​cases.

"This is a great day for Alabama parents. Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction. TikTok has agreed to give parents real control over what their kids see and how much time they spend on the app," Marshall said in a press release.
With this, the company has settled all cases selected for trial against it, including claims by five young people and a Kentucky school district.
What were the allegations against TikTok?

The state of Alabama had argued that TikTok's endless stream of videos makes it the most addictive of social media platforms and that its algorithm specifically pushes young users toward content about violence and self harm.
The state held the app partially responsible for a teen mental health crisis and a significant increase in emergency room visits.
The lawsuit also accused TikTok of falsely claiming that it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have the app rated as 'safe for teens' on app stores.
It said that TikTok asks users to self-report their ages but also allows them to evade questions by viewing videos without creating an account.
That still earns the company data on viewing habits. Being able to scroll videos without signing in makes 'Kids Mode' an entirely useless feature, the lawsuit said.
France debates social media ban for teenagers
What measures will TikTok take?
As per the settlement, TikTok has to implement a series of safety measures, including:

items: Two-hour daily limit
Additional parental control limiting time on platform
'Productive pauses' interrupting continuous scrolling after 15 minutes, 60 minutes and 90 minutes
Restrict children access from 12 a.m. to 6 a.m.
Restrictions on push notifications during night and school hours
Robust measures to verify user age
Limits on discoverability of teen accounts by adults
Sending parents notifications of suspicious interactions between teen users and adults
Blanket ban on use of cosmetic filters by teens
Non-personalized feed for teens

blocks.text: Last month, Meta agreed to pay a massive $17 billion to 47 US states and territories in a similar case while agreeing to make changes to teens' access to its platforms, Facebook and Instagram.
It did not admit wrongdoing and conditioned $5 billion of the payout on TikTok, Snap and YouTube's adoption of the same terms. TikTok has not commented publicly about that deal.
