articles.title: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
articles.summary: Climate change is transforming Papua's snowy peaks, which hold scientific value and spiritual significance.

blocks.text: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever
Image source, Project Pressure/Klaus Tymann
Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman Range
ByAbraham Utama
BBC Indonesia
The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.
The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.
They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.
But now, nearly all the snow is gone.
A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.
But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.

Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.

blocks.caption: Map and satellite image showing rapidly shrinking glaciers around Puncak Jaya in Indonesia's Papua region. Labels mark nearby peaks including Sumantri, Ngga Pulu and Carstensz East, with a callout noting that glaciers near the peaks are disappearing. An inset map locates Papua on the island of Ne…

blocks.text: "There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".

She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.
Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history.

Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.
But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936

blocks.text: The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936
Proof of a warming planet

The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.
As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.
El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.
The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.
A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.
The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems

blocks.text: Image source, Marie Šabacká
Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systems
A spiritual anchor
At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.
The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow".

"Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."
According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.
Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts.

"How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."

blocks.caption: Image caption, The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe

blocks.text: The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribe
For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.
The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.
Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.

Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded.
The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment.

"Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."

blocks.caption: Image caption, This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows where ice used to be in light blue

blocks.text: This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows where ice used to be in light blue
As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.
Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.
From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."
Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change.
"When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.
Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed.
"I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

articles.title: Liberal MP says he was demoted for supporting NDP bill targeting arms export controls
articles.summary: Charlottetown MP Sean Casey says he was removed from his position as parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs because he voted against the government and supported an NDP private…

image.caption: Liberal MP Sean Casey says he was warned against voting for an NDP MP's bill that would tighten Canada's arms export rules. While over a dozen Liberals ultimately did, he was the only parliamentary secretary among them. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Charlottetown MP Sean Casey says he was removed from his position as parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs because he voted against the government and supported an NDP private member's bill that targeted arms export controls.
P.E.I. MP says he was warned that move would mean losing parliamentary secretary role
· CBC News
· Posted: Sep 25, 2026 5:31 PM EDT | Last Updated: 28 minutes ago

Charlottetown MP Sean Casey says he was removed from his position as parliamentary secretary to the minister of veterans affairs because he supported an NDP private member's bill that targeted arms exports to Israel.
In March, Casey said he was warned by the Liberal whip that if he supported NDP MP Jenny Kwan's Bill C-233, known as the No More Loopholes Act, then he would be relieved of his duties.
Although 15 Liberal MPs broke rank and supported the bill, Casey was the only parliamentary secretary to do so.

"The bill was targeted at closing the loopholes that allowed for Canadian military equipment to be sold to another country but end up in Israel, so end up being used to kill Palestinians," said Casey in an interview with CBC News.

items: NDP's U.S. arms-control bill fails, 15 Liberal MPs break rank with government
Crown corp. reviewed U.S.-bound arms exports over potential transfer to Israel

blocks.text: "That was the goal of the legislation. And that's what my constituents were concerned about."

Casey said he received a call from the Atlantic desk of the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) on Thursday saying that he was being replaced. He described the conversations with both the whip and the PMO as "direct" and clearly referencing his support for Kwan's bill.
On Friday, the PMO announced that Quebec MP Sophie Chatel will replace Casey.
Parliamentary secretaries make $20,900 above their base MP salary of $217,700 and represent the minister at public events.
Casey said over the past six months, he began to wonder whether he'd be disciplined at all.
"I kept my word to my constituents and I voted in favour of the legislation and didn't hear anything from anyone until yesterday," he said.
"It took so darn long, I was kind of wondering if they forgot about me."
Departure from Trudeau platform

Casey said his understanding was that Liberal MPs outside of cabinet were entitled to a free vote on private member's bills, except in cases that involve implementing the Liberal platform, traditional confidence matters like the budget or instances that affected protections guaranteed in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
This was explicitly laid out in the 2015 Liberal platform that brought the Trudeau Liberals to power.
"Based on everything I knew in my 15 years here, there was a rule change that was unbeknownst to me and to many of my colleagues," he said.

The Prime Minister's Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The vote did not appear to be whipped, given that more than a dozen Liberal MPs did support Kwan's bill, which ultimately failed.
In a statement, Kwan said what happened to Casey is "distressing and should concern all Canadians."
She said it raises questions about the Liberal government's commitment to allowing MPs to exercise their judgment and represent their constituents freely.
"The prime minister talks a good talk, but in reality, he will wield his power to shut down dissent," she said.

Casey said this will not prevent him from reflecting the will of his constituents in the House, saying "if anything, I'm freed a little bit to not have to toe the party line as strictly as is now apparently required."
But he said he continues to have "tremendous" respect for the prime minister and affection for the Liberal Party.
"What has happened doesn't change that one iota," he said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McKenna is a senior reporter with CBC’s parliamentary bureau in Ottawa, where she covers federal politics. She previously worked for CBC’s The Fifth Estate and in the Halifax, Montreal and Charlottetown newsrooms. Her investigative and breaking news coverage has won five RTDNA awards. She is the author of No Choice: The 30-Year Fight for Abortion on Prince Edward Island.

articles.title: Yemeni leader calls for general mobilization against Houthis
articles.summary: Amid military escalation with the Iran-backed Houthis, the Saudi-backed head of Yemen's governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces.

image.caption: The civil war between the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and the Iran-backed Houthis has escalated sharply amid the Iran war Image: Marwan Abdullah Yahya Saeed Al-shabi/Anadolu/IMAGO

blocks.text: Rashad al-Alimi, the head of Yemen's Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council, on Friday called for a general mobilization in the war-torn country.

"I call upon the sons of our great people to engage in general mobilization and national mobilization, to rally around their armed and security forces," al-Alimi, who is also Supreme Commander of the Yemeni Armed Forces, said in a televised address.
The head of the governing body urged his compatriots to join the government forces weeks after Yemen's government was dealt a major blow by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels.

The Houthis have seized control of Yemen's entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive, allowing them to fully control the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait, igniting global fears about shipping through the chokepoint.
What else did Yemen's leader say?

In his address, al-Alimi also said that the objective of the mobilization is to "restore state institutions and extend sovereignty over the entire national territory," including the Yemeni capital of Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since 2014.
He added that anyone who defects from the Houthis to the government will be pardoned in an upcoming amnesty.
Al-Alimi addressed residents of Houthi-controlled areas, urging them to protect their children and not send them to fight alongside the Houthis.
"The state does not view you as a party to the conflict but as its people and partners," he said.
Why can't Saudi Arabia stop the Houthis?
Houthis escalate conflict

For more than a decade, the Houthis have been fighting Yemen's Saudi-backed government. Although a 2022 truce left the conflict largely frozen, fighting has recently flared up again amid the wider conflict involving Iran.

In recent weeks, the Houthis have intensified their missile and drone attacks on neighboring Saudi Arabia. They declared a maritime blockade and attacked Saudi targets in an attempt to stifle Saudi oil exports.
The Houthis accuse the kingdom of besieging Yemeni areas under their control. They attacked Riyadh for the first time in years over the weekend, marking a major escalation.

articles.title: Black woman found hanging from tree was dead before body was 'staged', police say
articles.summary: Tasia Fortune's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

blocks.text: Warning: This story contains distressing details
Police in the US state of Mississippi have said that they believe a black woman was already dead before her body was "staged" and placed hanging in a tree.
The disclosure was made in court by a detective on Friday, who also said they believed Tasia Fortune, a mother of four, had been killed in a dispute related to drugs.
The 29-year-old's body was found hanging from a tree on the grounds of an abandoned home in Jackson in August.

The discovery sparked widespread fears in the majority-black city, due to the state's deep history of racial violence and lynchings. After weeks of speculation and demands for information, police made multiple arrests.
In a news release, police said that the medical examiner had determined after an autopsy that Fortune's death was a homicide and that "the scene and the hanging were staged".
The BBC has contacted the court, the medical examiner's office and Fortune's mother, Christy Spivey.
Officials have not stated the exact cause of death or shared why they believe the hanging was staged.
The medical examiner confirmed earlier this month that Fortune's cause of death was homicide and said there would be a murder charge.
Speaking to reporters outside the Jackson Police Department on Friday, Fortune's mother described how she knows her daughter fought for her life till the very end.
"I know she did. I know my daughter," Spivey told reporters. Fortune leaves behind four young children, ages 7, 5, 4 and 1, she added.
Dressed in a shirt that reads "Justice for Tasia Fortune", Spivey stressed that she does not want to see any innocent people going to jail.
"I just hope they have the right people," she said.
Three people have been arrested in relation to the case, including Jarques Ratliff, 51, who was arrested and pleaded not guilty. He remains in custody in without bond.
A second person, Earnest Lloyd Jr, 25, was arrested in the case this week.
A third, 45-year-old Eric Clark, turned himself in to authorities on Friday and was charged with murder. He is scheduled to appear in court on Monday.

The 29-year-old's death is one of several cases in recent years that has prompted lawmakers to call on the justice department and the FBI to investigate all hanging deaths of black people in the country.
Representative Ayanna Pressley, Democrat of Massachusetts, cites at least 10 documented incidents in her September letter to Congress, external, which contained over 50 signatures from US lawmakers.
The most recent incident happened in Prince George's County, a majority-black suburb near Washington DC, on Sunday. It has been ruled a suicide.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran’s shows at Robert Kraft’s Gillette Stadium cancelled due to bad weather
articles.summary: Ed Sheeran’s concerts at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been cancelled due to severe weather warnings, the latest blow to a tour that has been surrounded by controversy since opener…

image.caption: Ed Sheeran, shown here performing during iHeartRadio KISS108's Jingle Ball 2025 in Boston, Massachusetts, will no longer be performing at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts this weekend due to bad weather. (Paras Griffin/Getty Images for for iHeartRadio)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Ed Sheeran’s concerts at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been cancelled due to severe weather warnings, the latest blow to a tour that has been surrounded by controversy since opener Macklemore was dropped for his pro-Palestinian comments on stage.
Cancellations are latest blow to Sheeran's tour

Ed Sheeran’s concerts at Gillette Stadium in Massachusetts have been cancelled due to severe weather warnings, the latest blow to a tour that has been mired in controversy since opener Macklemore was dropped for on-stage pro-Palestinian comments.

Earlier this month, Macklemore was dropped from the tour's U.S. leg after stadium owners including billionaire Robert Kraft threatened to cancel Sheeran's shows if the rapper remained on the lineup, triggering an exodus as Sheeran’s remaining openers pulled out in solidarity.

Now, Sheeran will no longer be performing at Kraft’s Gillette Stadium on Friday and Saturday. Local weather reports are calling for a storm with gusts of wind up to 64 kilometres per hour in Foxborough, where the stadium is located, outside of Boston.

“Due to the severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England throughout the weekend and following consultation with local officials, we have made the difficult decision to cancel the Ed Sheeran concerts at Gillette Stadium,” Messina Touring, Sheeran’s touring group, said in an Instagram statement. The venue shared the same statement.
All tickets will be refunded through their point of purchase, the touring group added.

The cancellation comes a day after Macklemore announced a new tour of his own, with proceeds going to organizations supporting Palestinians. He slammed what he called “the billionaire class” deciding “which voices are allowed on stage and which ones are too dangerous to hear,” quipping that his schedule had recently “freed up a bit” since being dropped as an opener.
"It’s 2026. Being apolitical during a genocide doesn’t work anymore," he wrote.
An independent UN commission and Amnesty International have concluded that Israel's actions against Palestinians in Gaza amount to genocide, which the country has consistently denied.
Macklemore played 2 shows before being dropped

Before being pulled from the roster, Macklemore had played two shows in early September at New Jersey’s MetLife Stadium for the U.S. leg of Sheeran's Loop Tour. In speeches during those sets, he chanted, “Free Palestine” to a cheering crowd and expressed solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the Israeli-occupied West Bank.

Kraft, owner of the New England Patriots and their home base Gillette Stadium, was one of those behind the push for Macklemore’s removal, according to Messina, Macklemore and Sheeran, who said he spoke on the phone with Kraft during discussions about the push to remove the rapper.
Sheeran has said the decision was solely due to venues and promoters, and that they would not change their minds.
In a statement about Macklemore's removal, Sheeran said he was "appalled by the conflict" but defended his choice not to take a public stance.

items: Macklemore announces new tour in support of Palestine
Why Ed Sheeran's response to the criticism fell short
Ms. Rachel pledges $1M US in Palestinian aid to match Macklemore's donation following Sheeran tour exit

blocks.text: Kraft told CBC News in a statement at the time that due to Macklemore’s New Jersey shows and “a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric,” he believed performances at Gillette Stadium would “cross that line.”
The rapper was also widely criticized in 2014 for wearing a Halloween costume that many said was antisemitic. He apologized for the incident at the time.
Openers Lukas Graham, Aaron Rowe and Finneas pulled out of the tour after Macklemore’s ousting, as did Sheeran’s backing band, Irish group Beoga.
“We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed.… Money doesn’t give you the right to own the conversation,” Graham wrote on Instagram.
Fans seeking refunds
The Gillette tour dates would have been Sheeran's second and third shows since losing his supporting acts.

At his first show without the acts on Sept. 19 at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Sheeran apologized to the crowd, saying he never wanted to be an "activist musician" and that "what is happening in Gaza is catastrophic and unjustifiable." He added that he is "listening and learning."

Pro-Palestinian protesters outside the venue called on other fans to boycott the show, criticizing Sheeran's apolitical stance. Prices have also sagged for remaining tickets since the controversy began.
Prior to the total cancellation of the Massachusetts shows, the state's attorney general had said that consumers looking for refunds due to the lineup changes would be granted them.

“After hearing from nearly 200 consumers who were struggling to obtain refunds from Ticketmaster for Ed Sheeran’s shows at Gillette Stadium this weekend, my office jumped into action to demand that consumers be provided a clear path to get their money back if they no longer want to attend due to significant changes to the lineup,” Andrea Joy Campbell said in a statement.

Ticketmaster's policy allows for openers to change without requiring that audiences be eligible for refunds. But Campbell said after her office submitted a request to the company, it made an exception for the Sept. 25 and 26 shows.
Did Ed Sheeran’s concert statement meet the moment?
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Alexandra Mae Jones is a senior writer for CBC News based in Toronto. She has written on a variety of topics, from health to pop culture to breaking news, and previously reported for CTV News and the Toronto Star. She joined CBC in 2024. You can reach her at alexandra.mae.jones@cbc.ca

articles.title: Hawaii readies for arrival of Hurricane Nolo amid risks of catastrophic flooding
articles.summary: Residents on Hawaii's Big Island were bracing Friday for potentially life-threatening and catastrophic flooding from Hurricane Nolo, while Mexico was still under the threat of Hurricane Polo as it…

image.caption: Ryanna Fry takes a picture of clouds in Kona, Hawaii, on Friday. Residents on Hawaii's Big Island were bracing Friday for potentially life-threatening and catastrophic flooding from Hurricane Nolo. (Gregory Bull/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Residents on Hawaii's Big Island were bracing Friday for potentially life-threatening and catastrophic flooding from Hurricane Nolo, while Mexico was still under the threat of Hurricane Polo as it headed toward the Baja Peninsula after bringing storm conditions to the southwestern coast.
Mexico remains under threat from Hurricane Polo as it heads toward Baja Peninsula

Nolo's maximum sustained winds have increased to 165 kilometres an hour, making it a Category 2 hurricane. The storm's centre was located about 300 kilometres south of South Point, Hawaii and about 610 kilometres south-southeast of Honolulu. It was moving north-northeast at about eight kilometres an hour.

Tropical storm conditions expected to begin on land in the evening, with hurricane conditions possible by early Saturday, the U.S. National Hurricane Center said. It was expected to take a turn west Saturday and avoid directly hitting the islands.
Forecasters warned eastern and southern areas of the island could see rainfall totals of 25 to 38 centimetres, with a maximum of 64 centimetres. Wind gusts on land could hit 80 kilometres an hour.
Nolo was expected to strengthen to a major hurricane on Saturday.

"People are going to want to kind of shelter in place on the Big Island, be in their safe place, certainly by later today, tonight, well into Saturday," Michael Brennan, director of the National Hurricane Center, said Friday.
"Don't venture out if you don't have to into the dangerous flooding environment, but also high winds. We can have trees and power lines down."
Heavy rainfall possible elsewhere
Heavy rainfall also was possible on Hawaii's other islands, the hurricane centre said. Maui also could see heavy rainfall and potential life-threatening flooding and mudslides, forecasters said.

Crews on the Big Island spent hours Friday trying to build berms to guide water and move large debris ahead of the worst of the rain, said Erika Kapu, Hawaii program manager for the humanitarian non-profit CORE.

Hawaii officials told residents to put together emergency kits and the governor issued an emergency proclamation, activating more than 230 Hawaii National Guard members. Schools were closed in some areas.

Hawaii County officials on the Big Island were urging residents in flood-prone areas to consider taking refuge at shelters being set up or other locations. Authorities said sand for sandbags was publicly available at several locations.

items: Southwestern Mexico braces for arrival of 'extremely dangerous' Hurricane Polo

blocks.text: The heaviest rain from Nolo is likely to fall over the same southeastern region of the Big Island that was hit in August by Hurricane Lala and where grounds are still wet from additional precipitation. The storm surge could hit 30 to 91 centimetres, creating large and dangerous waves and coastal flooding, the hurricane centre said.
Residents and tourists on the Big Island were busy preparing.
"I guess that'd be my concern — whether we're getting out of here or not, but, you know, as far as the weather goes, it is what it is," said Daniel Compton, who was visiting from Seattle.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green has requested an emergency disaster declaration for four Hawaii counties.
Polo gaining strength

The hurricane centre said Polo gained significant force overnight into Friday morning and doused parts of Mexico's Pacific coast. No major damage or flooding was reported along the coast overnight into Friday.

By midday Friday, attention turned to the Baja California Peninsula, where the hurricane was slated to arch back and hit between Monday and Tuesday. Local authorities were preparing shelters. Mexico's government announced Friday afternoon that they were closing ports in the region as dark clouds swirled overhead.
The latest estimated sustained winds were 290 kilometres an hour.

Residents stacked sandbags to fortify beachfront shops and evacuated their homes in some coastal areas on Thursday. Mexican authorities opened shelters and cleared people from beaches, and 15,000 security personnel were deployed across the coast. Schools were closed.

In the port city of Lázaro Cárdenas in Michoacán, seawater swept through homes and left wooden planks and furniture strewn on the streets. Locals and government officials were clearing debris and shoveling thick mud coating much of the town.

Alicia Contreras said the walls and roof of her restaurant had been severely damaged by 4.5-metre waves. As officers and family helped pick through the damage, Contreras worried about how she would recover economically.
"This is huge because we have no other source of income. Now we're just surviving," Contreras said.

Brennan said some moisture associated with Polo will be pushed into parts of the southwestern U.S. by Monday, possibly producing scattered flash flooding in the Four Corners region, particularly portions of Arizona and New Mexico.
El Niño prompts global shifts

El Niño is prompting major environmental shifts across the world, fuelling drought in some areas and flooding in others. It traditionally dampens the Atlantic hurricane season, while it tends to rev up tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific with moist air and little wind shear.
A third storm in the Pacific, Hurricane Odalys, was at Category 4 status and was still far from land, roughly 1,537 kilometres west-southwest of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula.
LISTEN | Will our weather always be like this?:
What on Earth?25:02Is this Super El Niño a peek into forever weather?
Two other powerful storms were churning in the Atlantic Ocean, but were not near land.

In the northern Atlantic, Tropical Storm Fay reformed early Thursday. As of Friday, it was about 1,674 kilometres west-southwest of the Azores, the hurricane centre said. Off Africa's western coast, Tropical Storm Gonzalo strengthened early Friday as it approached the Cabo Verde Islands.

articles.title: Trump Avenue sign goes missing before official name change
articles.summary: Even before Ottawa city council could get around to removing U.S. President Donald Trump's name from a local residential street, it appears someone has beaten them to it.

image.caption: The Trump Avenue sign at the corner with Whitestone Drive in Ottawa has gone missing. (Mathieu Deroy/CBC)

blocks.text: Ottawa·Updated
Even before Ottawa city council could get around to removing U.S. President Donald Trump's name from a local residential street, it appears someone has beaten them to it.
Street sign disappears 2 days after council votes to remove U.S. president's name

On Friday afternoon, the blue and white Trump Avenue sign at the corner of Whitestone Drive in Ottawa's Central Park neighbourhood was missing. Its absence had been flagged on social media earlier in the day.
Other Trump Avenue signs in the area remain.
CBC News reached out to the City of Ottawa to ask if the sign was stolen or removed by the city, and if so when.

The city replied via email that it's looking into what happened and that once the city has "confirmed the status of the sign," staff will figure out next steps, including whether a replacement is needed.
CBC News has also reached out to Ottawa police for more information.
Ottawa's Central Park area features other New York City-themed names such as Bloomingdale Street and Staten Way.
The sign's mysterious disappearance comes just two days after Ottawa city councillors voted to rename the street, which was named after Trump 20 years ago, before he became president.
River ward Coun. Riley Brockington fronted the motion to change the name earlier this month, saying the American president doesn't deserve the honour in light of his repeated threats to Canada.

The motion came after Trump imposed tariffs on many billions of dollars worth of Canadian goods and signed an order to rename Lake Ontario to Lake America. Canada has retaliated with tariffs on an equivalent value of U.S. imports.
That motion was approved on Wednesday.

items: Ottawa city council votes to dump Trump Avenue

blocks.text: A working group will be formed to consult with the public, go over options and come up with a new name to be voted on next spring, Brockington said.

A previous effort to rename Trump Avenue in 2021 failed after a consultation found residents split on the idea, with many who opposed the change expressing concerns about the inconvenience of changing their home address.
The City of Ottawa has a program for buying decommissioned signs for streets whose names have been renamed.
You can learn more about that here.
In its email, the city said street signs are "a critical piece of infrastructure for reporting and responding to emergencies" and that they should not be removed, damaged or taken.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
guy.quenneville@cbc.ca
With files from Mathieu Deroy, David Fraser and Arthur White-Crummey

articles.title: Lula or Bolsonaro as president? Brazil gears up to vote
articles.summary: Brazilians go to the polls on October 4. The front-runners are multilateralist incumbent Lula da Silva and former President Jair Bolsonaro's son, Flavio, who wants to bring Brazil closer to the US…

image.caption: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva (seen at left and right) is facing off with Flavio Bolsonaro (center)Image: Sergio Lima/AFP

blocks.text: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva spoke in no uncertain terms at the opening of the UN General Assembly on Tuesday in New York: "Brazil does not belong in anyone's backyard," the Brazilian president said. His comment was directed at his US counterpart Donald Trump, despite Trump not being in attendance.

The US president has repeatedly interfered with Brazilian domestic politics, siding with former President Jair Messias Bolsonaro and the far-right opposition. In July, Trump imposed sanctions on a judge who found Bolsonaro guilty of attempting a coup and sentenced him to 27 years in jail. Washington only lifted the sanctions after negotiating with Lula.
Bolsonaro's eldest son Flavio is Lula's biggest challenger in the upcoming presidential election on October 4, and polls currently show the two of them to be neck and neck in a potential runoff.

The election in the world's fifth largest country is drawing a great deal of international attention. Brazil is an agricultural giant and very rich in natural resources — boasting rare earth elements, vast water resources and enormous crude oil reserves.
Brazil one of South America's last bastions of the left

Lula is the "last man standing" of the South American left, while Flavio Bolsonaro is part of an increasingly strong far-right camp. Argentina, Bolivia, Peru, Chile, Ecuador and Colombia all have governments that are sympathetic to Trump. And since January, Venezuela has been what some describe as a US protectorate.

blocks.caption: Lula advocates for multilateralist diplomacy and good international relations with all countriesImage: Silvia Izquierdo/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Foreign policy hasn't played a big role in the campaign, but this election will nonetheless decide whether Brazil moves closer to Trump's US. Washington is seeking economic and military dominance in South America through the Shield of the Americas initiative, focused on combating violent cartels. After his military intervention in Venezuela, Trump is now exerting economic pressure on Mexico and Cuba. At the same time, he is trying to counter Chinese influence in the region.
For his part, Lula is an advocate of multilateralist diplomacy, wanting Brazil to engage in dialogue and trade with everybody. China has long been Brazil's most important trading partner.

Flavio Bolsonaro favors a conservative alliance with the US and other right-wing states. But for Leonardo Paz from the Brazilian Fundacao Getulio Vargas think tank, a Bolsonaro victory would not necessarily automatically mean better relations with the US. He told DW that Lula had established a largely normal relationship with Trump — both are 80 years old — despite some initial friction. The two leaders got along well, said Paz, even if Lula has not succumbed to Trump's pressure.
Who is Brazil's Flavio Bolsonaro?

Paz did admit that if Bolsonaro won, the 45-year-old would be more likely to accommodate Trump, pointing out that his father Jair had made far-reaching concessions to the US when he was president. During Jair Bolsonaro's time in office from 2019 to 2023, Brazil agreed to forgo its "developing country status" in World Trade Organization negotiations in exchange for a mere promise that the US would back its bid to become a member of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Trump also said he was considering giving Brazil NATO "privileges." Neither promise came to anything.

"While relations with the US would continue as they are with Lula, it is completely unclear what a Flavio Bolsonaro presidency would mean," Rubens Ricupero, a former Brazilian diplomat and minister, told DW. "Lula has prestige in foreign policy, while Bolsonaro is completely inexperienced."
Would Brazil pull out of BRICS?

A victory for Bolsonaro would likely jeopardize Brazil's role in BRICS, the alliance that comprises Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa and five other states. Bolsonaro has said that one of his first acts would be to review whether Brazil should stay in the alliance, arguing that BRICS only serves to provoke the US. He has also spoken out against China's efforts to reduce the global dominance of the US dollar.

It's hard to tell how serious such intentions are, considering the importance of economic ties between China and Brazil. Javier Milei, Argentina's current president, also engaged in harsh rhetoric against China before he came to power, but quickly adopted a more conciliatory tone once in office to not jeopardize Chinese loans.
"Political relations with China would likely cool, but I wouldn't expect any substantial changes in economic and commercial relations," predicted Ricupero in case of a Bolsonaro victory.

Paz agreed that Flavio Bolsonaro was unlikely to take an extremely aggressive stance toward China in case of victory. He explained that, like Milei, Jair Bolsonaro had engaged in some sharp rhetoric against Beijing at the beginning of his term but had quickly softened his tone, given the fact that Brazil's agricultural sector in particular is so dependent on China.

Paz pointed out that the Bolsonaro family enjoyed most support in Brazil's rural regions, which made good money with China. "The unknown factor with Flavio Bolsonaro is how much pressure the US would exert so that Brazil distanced itself from China and to what extent he would yield to the pressure," said Paz.

blocks.caption: If he wins, Flavio Bolsonaro is expected to dismantle policies that protect the environment Image: Bruna Prado/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Brazil not likely to become major world player

Paz said that despite possessing enormous natural resources that are important to the global economy, Brazil would likely remain a minor player on the world stage as it had neither the economic strength to provide financial aid to other countries nor the military strength to help resolve conflicts. "This severely limits Brazil's ability to act," he said.

But Brazil could continue to be a major protagonist in the Global South, he said, as it is under Lula. "This is particularly evident in the international debate on global governance, in which Brazil raises issues such as new trading conditions, climate policy and development," he said.

blocks.caption: Bolsonaro supporters, seen here with a Trump inflatable at a rally on September 7, favor a Brazil that is close to Trump's US Image: Alexandre Meneghini/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ricupero said Lula carried particular weight in foreign policy, especially regarding the environment and climate change. "His commitment to addressing ecological challenges was clear from his choice of [leading environmentalist] Marina Silva as environment minister," he said.

The former diplomat said he feared Flavio Bolsonaro would repeat the mistakes of his father, and this was one of the reasons the election was drawing such attention from around the world. He pointed out that Brazil had become more isolated after Jair Bolsonaro dismantled major environmental policies, adding that relations with the European Union had particularly suffered and negotiations on a trade agreement between Mercosur and the bloc had been put on hold. The deal was finally signed early this year.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Marineland belugas that died in Chicago had chronic inflammatory disease, preliminary necropsy findings show
articles.summary: Post-mortem examinations for two former Marineland belugas indicate the whales were sick when they arrived at their new home at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago. Peekachu, 23, and Rain, 20, were part of a…

image.caption: CBC News flew a drone over Marineland in August and observed staff feeding and interacting with belugas and dolphins before they were relocated to aquariums in the U.S. and Spain. (Patrick Morrell/ CBC)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Post-mortem examinations for two former Marineland belugas indicate the whales were sick when they arrived at their new home at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago. Peekachu, 23, and Rain, 20, were part of a massive operation to rehome 30 belugas and four dolphins from Niagara Falls, Ont., to aquariums in the U.S. and Spain this summer.
Fisheries and Oceans Canada cites ‘unacceptable neglect’ of Niagara Falls, Ont., whales' health
Post-mortem examinations of two former Marineland belugas indicate the whales were sick when they arrived last month at their new home at Shedd Aquarium in Chicago.

Peekachu, 23, and Rain, 20, arrived on Aug. 13 as part of a massive operation to rehome 30 belugas and four dolphins from Niagara Falls, Ont., to four aquariums in the U.S. and one in Spain. The moves took place in six stages this summer.
Preliminary medical findings “identified significant, chronic gastrointestinal disease,” according to a Shedd Aquarium release on the two whales’ deaths.
“The disease had likely been present for an extended period,” according to the aquarium, due to “the significance of the inflammation, the types of immune cells present” and other signs.

items: 4 Marineland belugas, 1 dolphin, died after being transferred. Why the rest remain on 'death watch'

blocks.text: “These changes develop over time, potentially months or years, indicating that the disease began before the whales arrived at Shedd and compromised their health rendering them more vulnerable and sensitive,” said the statement.
Rocks among foreign objects in stomachs

Examinations on the female belugas also revealed foreign materials in their stomachs, including “bird feathers, sticks and large, porous rocks” in Peekachu, and “small flecks of material that may be paint” in Rain.
In the case of Peekachu, “she could not have ingested these materials while at Shedd, and they are believed to have been present before her rescue,” said the statement.
Shedd said it doesn’t believe the foreign materials were directly related to their passing. The necropsy also found no evidence of communicable disease.

items: Marineland dolphin dies at Spain aquarium, marking 5th death after rescue transfer

blocks.text: Marineland, the permanently closed theme park and zoo, threatened to euthanize the animals last fall, writing at the time that it was running out of money to care for them.
Another female beluga, 26-year-old Osiris, also died after arriving at Shedd Aquarium, but necropsy results aren’t currently available.

Two other former Marineland animals ‒ Jelly Bean, a 19-year-old beluga, and Echo, a 30-year-old bottlenose dolphin ‒ also died, after being rehomed to Oceanogràfic de València in Spain. Post-mortems are also being done in these cases.
Ottawa cites apparent 'neglect' of whales

A statement from Canada’s Ministry of Fisheries and Oceans, the federal body in charge of approving export of the belugas and dolphins, said the preliminary necropsy findings reveal “an unacceptable neglect for their health and well-being prior to their relocation.”

It added that “we continue to be grateful to the experienced professionals who have played a role in this operation, helping provide a dignified last chapter to these whales and supporting many others in their new homes.”
CBC's Aarti Pole talks to Valeria Vergara about concerns over the recent death of a Marineland beluga.

In its statement, Shedd Aquarium said Peekachu and Rain “came to Shedd from a facility, where provincial authorities had repeatedly documented environmental concerns… Shedd understood that some whales could arrive with serious, long-standing health needs that could in no way be fully assessed before the rescue.”
‘I'm still expecting more of these whales to die’
Camille Labchuk, executive director of Animal Justice, questioned whether the whales were healthy enough to be moved.
“And I think that's something that experts should have detected beforehand,” said Labchuk.
She said her group has been warning the federal and provincial governments for years that at some point, Marineland would close and the whales would need to be moved.
“There should have been a lot more diligence years ago to get these whales into a healthier condition so… they could have survived the move without paying the price with their lives.”
“This was a slow-moving disaster that everybody saw coming,” said Labchuck, “I'm still expecting more of these whales to die.”
CBC News reached out to Marineland for comment and will update this story with any response.
With files from CBC Hamilton

articles.title: Why the viral clip of 'multitasking mom' at a baseball game has enraged people online
articles.summary: A woman with a baby strapped to her chest, a diaper bag on her back, and her arms full of food at a Major League Baseball game has inadvertently become a metaphor for the disproportionate load…

image.caption: A screengrab of a video posted to X that shows the woman carrying a baby, diaper bag and trays of food in the stands at Oracle Park in San Francisco. (@nocontextsfg/X)

blocks.text: World·New

A woman with a baby strapped to her chest, a diaper bag on her back, and her arms full of food at a Major League Baseball game has inadvertently become a metaphor for the disproportionate load mothers carry — in this case, literally.
Video of woman carrying baby, diaper bag, trays of food toward waiting man draws disbelief and scorn

The woman was singled out by two legendary broadcasters at Tuesday's game between the Giants and the Twins at Oracle Park in San Francisco as she sidestepped back toward her seat balancing three trays of food.
"Holy smokes, Mike! Look at this," Duane Kuiper says as the woman makes her way across the aisle.
"If there's ever a true definition of a multitasking mother, that is the deal right there," Mike Krukow responds in the broadcast.

The clip, which has since gone viral, shows the man in the seat next to the "multitasking mother" staring at his phone until the woman is nearly beside him, standing up to move a coat out of her seat, then digging into his food while the woman shrugs the diaper bag off her back, still holding the grinning baby and two full trays.
"Did I just hear that guy say, 'Did you forget something?'" Kuiper asks, as the two broadcasters joke that maybe he she didn't bring any ketchup.

The broadcast returned to her a few more times between pitches while Kuiper and Krukow expressed disbelief at the scene, exclaiming, "are you kidding me?" and "bless her heart" as the man popped some fried food in his mouth.
"Well, that’s mom of the year right there!" Krukow said.
"She’ll be the last one to eat, too," added Kuiper.
Neither the woman nor the man sitting beside her have been identified. CBC News has contacted the San Francisco Giants and NBC for comment, but has yet to hear back.
Visual of a familiar sentiment
Without hearing from the people involved, observers can't know the context of the situation — like whether the man is her partner, or whether or not help was offered.

But while some have argued you can't judge a situation based on a short clip, for many others, "multitasking mom" represents invisible labour, the mental load of motherhood, and weaponized incompetence.
"How do I divorce someone else’s husband?" one person asked in the comments of an ESPNW Instagram reel of the clip viewed 40 million times by Friday. The comment was "liked" nearly 115,000 times.
"Let us stop normalizing this," someone else commented.

items: Despite gains, women still do most of the housework. Will this gender gap ever narrow?
Did 'Marathon Mom' ignore her kids? Why a viral video is enraging runners and mothers

blocks.text: The clip is resonating because it gave a visual to a familiar sentiment — that women do more household labour and family management, explained Shana MacDonald, the O'Donovan Chair in communication at the University of Waterloo, who researches social and digital media.
"This showed that in a very direct but almost comical way," she told CBC News.

On a broader scale, the past year has seen a significant increase in conversations around motherhood, MacDonald added. Some parts of society are emphasizing motherhood as "womens' central calling," she noted, while in other spheres, we're hearing more concerns about burnout and lack of support.
That includes some of the recent conversations about Lindsay Clancy, the U.S. mom who was on trial for the deaths of her three children, MacDonald said.
How social media drives toxic obsession with the Lindsay Clancy case
Clip is triggering for many: sociology prof

The clip from the Giants game offers people a chance to voice their frustrations, Lisa Strohschein, a sociology professor at the University of Alberta and editor-in-chief of the journal Canadian Studies in Population, told CBC News.
She cautioned people against rendering judgments without knowing any of the context, while adding that the clip has tapped into the anger about structural inequalities in our society.
In the U.S., for instance, reproductive rights are being rolled back, she noted, and so-called "trad wives" that glamourize domestic life are on the rise.

In Canada, while some studies have found that fathers are taking on more parenting than they have in the past, others have found mothers are still generally the managers of the household. Women also still consistently take on a larger share of unpaid household work, including chores and child care, according to a 2022 Statistics Canada report.
All that to say, a woman balancing trays of dinner and a baby while a man next to her eats seems to be triggering for a lot of people, Strohschein said.
"Women, when they see this — I think it's kind of like the last straw."
What is the 'motherhood penalty'?
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Taylor Swift dropped 4 new songs. Here's what fans are sleuthing
articles.summary: If there’s one thing guaranteed to turn the internet into a room full of amateur detectives, it’s a new Taylor Swift track. Make that four and they go full-blown CSI. The pop star dropped The Life of…

image.caption: Newly released image for Taylor Swift's The Life of a Showgirl: Encore (Instagram/Taylorswift/TAS Management)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

If there’s one thing guaranteed to turn the internet into a room full of amateur detectives, it’s a new Taylor Swift track. Make that four and they go full-blown CSI. The pop star dropped The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, the extended version of her 2025 album that includes four new tracks.
The pop star dropped the extended version of her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl on Friday
If there’s one thing guaranteed to turn the internet into a room full of amateur detectives, it’s a new Taylor Swift track. Make that four and they go full-blown CSI.
The pop star dropped The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, the extended version of her 2025 album that includes four new tracks.

It's part of a broader trend of pop artists releasing an extension of their album as a deluxe, with experts speculating it is done to boost streaming revenue, or sell more units as physical media makes a comeback. Artists like Sabrina Carpenter, Olivia Rodrigo, Zara Larsson and Charli XCX have all done the same.
Swift says the new tracks came together after she went to Sweden to celebrate the success of The Life of a Showgirl with collaborators Max Martin and Shellback.
All four songs have since charted in the Top 10 on Apple Music but have been receiving mixed reviews, with some Swifties expressing letdown over the star's output.
"As a Swift fan, I find the four new songs quite disappointing," one fan wrote on X.
"I guess this era isn’t really just for me," another wrote on Instagram. "NO ITS SO SO GOOD," a third commented.
We scrubbed through the internet to find out what fans are thinking. Shall we dive into the rumour mill? Let's go track by track.
Patient Zero
This is the lead single, she announced the other day on Instagram.

On first listen, fans think this one puts Swift in the role of "patient zero," and that she seems to be talking to an ex's new partner, singing: "I've been there. Felt the reeling, done the healing," and, "If he’s killing you, I see you. I was patient zero.”
Some speculate it could be Sofie Turner and Joe Jonas, who Taylor Swift also dated way back when. But fear not: Swift herself confirmed the meaning to Capital FM radio Friday.

“I was hanging out with a bunch of friends, and one of my friends told us that she had been reached out to by the new girlfriend of an ex of hers, asking for guidance on if she had had the same experiences with this guy that this new girlfriend was having,” Swift told the station.
“And everyone in our group just immediately started saying like, 'Oh, I've been through that too,' and telling the stories of when this kind of reach-out had happened for them.”
A music video for the song will air at this weekend's MTV VMAs, starring Dakota Johnson and Colin Farrell.
Cleveland!

It doesn't require much decoding to decipher the subject of this song as Swift's husband Travis Kelce. The two got married at Madison Square Garden earlier this year. Fans think she's speaking to her critics in this one.
"He already took me to Cleveland and showed me The Heights," she pens. "And now I'm wearing white, so hate all you like this is the love of my life."
Its simplistic lyrics have Swifties spinning, some upset with her output.
"Cleveland … we need to talk," one user wrote on X. Others are coming to her defence. "Cleveland is corny and THANK GOD IT IS!!!!!!" wrote another.
Pink Clouding
This song seems to be a lyrical apology for being a "liar" in a previous relationship.
“Years later, I still wonder how to tell you sorry,” Swift sings.

Many fans are theorizing it's a message to Tom Hiddleston because of its apparent callbacks to songs from her catalogue like Getaway Car, which fans also think is about Hiddleston. The two were briefly coupled up in 2016.

“Having a Taylor Swift song about Tom Hiddleston in the big 2026 feels like sleeping with a cold pillow,” one user wrote. “Didn’t expect a hiddleswift apology in the year of 2026 i love her bad,” wrote another.
Babylon
Thing is, even Swifties can't pin down exactly what this one is about.
"Am I stupid what is she trying to say in Babylon," one fan wrote on X. "I have no idea what Taylor Swift is singing about in Babylon, but it’s my favourite movie of the year," wrote another.
A look at the lyrics tells you it's about a person who left their small town in Virginia, having regrets at a casino and on a train.
"You never knew that it was Babylon 'til it was gone," Swift writes, leading some to believe it's a message about nostalgia.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Griffin Jaeger is a reporter and producer with CBC's entertainment unit. He also formerly hosted and produced content for The National’s digital platforms. You can reach him at griffin.jaeger@cbc.ca

blocks.text: Montreal·New

· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Sep 25, 2026 2:31 PM EDT | Last Updated: 14 minutes ago
Coalition Avenir Québec Leader Christine Fréchette told journalists she reached out to Prime Minister Mark Carney and requested a meeting with him to discuss the matter.
She was reacting to a news report published by Québecor media outlets that said American officials had attempted to negotiate directly with Quebec government officials regarding tariffs.
"I want to ensure that the full truth about this issue comes to light," Fréchette said on the campaign trail. "[The election] must remain in the hands of and be decided by the people of Quebec."
Canada's foreign affairs minister, Anita Anand, said at a news conference in Ottawa that the federal government is taking the issue very seriously.
"Protecting our democracy is of the utmost importance to our country," she said.
She added that she will speak with her American counterpart, Marco Rubio, after reviewing evidence of the allegations.
"Right now I have not seen the evidence," Anand said.

articles.title: Trump's plans for massive arch move ahead
articles.summary: Opposition to building the 250-foot arch, and using it for military purposes, is growing with one Democrat blasting Trump's plans as "foolhardy".

blocks.text: Earlier this week Trump announced that the proposed "Triumphal Arch" would double as a complex to store military equipment, complete with the ability to deploy snipers and drones from the roof and plaza.
In a letter to the Pentagon and Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), Duckworth said they "must reject this foolhardy plan and instead focus on increasing the safety of the airspace".

The arch is to be built just outside Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia, and about 4mi (6km) from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, the site of the deadly 2025 midair crash between a military helicopter and commercial plane.

"The American people cannot afford to stand witness to Trump's risky plan to place a 250-foot (72m) structure along a busy approach path, especially if he follows through on plans to station snipers on the arch and fly drones," Duckworth wrote in the letter, which was obtained by the BBC's US partner, CBS News.
The FAA, however, ruled last week that the massive structure would not pose a risk to flights coming into and out of the airport.

On Thursday, the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation, led by Trump appointees, announced it was ending required consultations with local officials about how the structure might affect 42 historic properties in the area.

The council said in the announcement that the National Park Service, which oversees federal landmarks, had proposed a plan for mitigating potential harms to those properties, but local historic preservation officers "raised concerns with the purpose and need of the Triumphal Arch". They also questioned whether the service had adequately identified possible harms and planned sufficient actions to address them.

Federal and state officials are not required to reach an agreement on a project's harm-mitigation plans, and those consultations are allowed to be terminated if both sides can't agree. The council expects to submit a final report on the process early next month.
Meanwhile, Democratic Virginia Congressman Don Beyer says excavation work on the site where the arch will stand has already begun.

Beyer, who is leading congressional opposition to the arch, said he found workers operating heavy equipment when he visited the site on Thursday who told him they were "conducting archaeological work to evaluate the composition of the soil".
That is "deeply troubling", Beyer said, particularly because the administration is required to give 48 hours notice before work can begin.
"The Administration appears to be pushing ahead with activity at the site even while it still has not done the basic work necessary to understand the consequences of this project," Beyer wrote.

A rendering of the design from earlier this year includes a golden, winged Lady Liberty on the top of the arch, flanked by two gold eagles, and with the phrases "One Nation Under God" and "Liberty and Justice for All" inscribed in gold on either side of the structure.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What to know about the new law moving the BSKE to 2028
articles.summary: MANILA -- President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has signed into law a measure postponing the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) originally scheduled for November 2, 2026.

blocks.text: Published September 26, 2026 2:06am
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has signed into law a measure postponing the Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE) originally scheduled for November 2, 2026.
Republic Act No. 12326 moves the next regular BSKE to the second Monday of November 2028, with succeeding elections to be held every five years thereafter.
The law also fixes the term of office of elected barangay and SK officials at five years.
Other key provisions include limiting elective barangay officials to two consecutive terms in the same position and elective SK officials to one term in the same position.
Marcos said the additional time in office should be used by incumbent officials to improve public service, complete ongoing programs and address the needs of their communities.

“Sa paglagda natin sa Republic Act No. 12326, na nagtatakda ng limang taong termino para sa mga opisyal ng barangay at Sangguniang Kabataan, malinaw ang ating inaasahan sa ating mga kasalukuyang opisyal,” Marcos said in a Facebook post.
(With the signing of Republic Act No. 12326, which sets a five-year term for barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials, our expectations for our current officials are clear.)

“Gamitin ang panahong ito upang mas pagbutihin ang serbisyo, tapusin ang mga nasimulang programa at mas tutukan ang pangangailangan ng bawat komunidad, pamilya at kabataan. Hindi ito dagdag na panahon sa puwesto. Dagdag itong panahon ng pananagutan sa taumbayan,” he added.

(Use this time to further improve public service, complete programs that have already been started, and focus more closely on the needs of every community, family, and young person. This is not additional time in office. It is additional time for accountability to the people.)
Previous postponements
The postponement marks another change to the schedule of the barangay and SK elections under the Marcos administration.
On October 10, 2022, months after assuming office, Marcos signed Republic Act No. 11935, postponing the December 2022 BSKE to October 2023.
The Supreme Court declared RA 11935 unconstitutional in June 2023 even as it allowed the October 30, 2023 elections to proceed.

The next BSKE was initially scheduled for December 1, 2025. The timeline was later changed when Marcos signed RA 12232 on August 13, 2025, setting the next regular barangay and SK elections for the first Monday of November 2026, or November 2.
Marcos later cited the need to focus on the inaugural parliamentary elections of the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM), which were also rescheduled to September 2026.
The barangay and SK elections have been repeatedly postponed since 2016.
Comelec preparations
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) had already begun preparations for the November 2026 BSKE, including the implementation of its election calendar.

Comelec Chairman George Erwin Garcia said the poll body could not halt its preparations based solely on pending legislation, as it had to remain ready in case the measure did not pass or faced a temporary restraining order after enactment.
Comelec had reportedly spent about P8 billion on preparations for the 2026 polls.

Following the enactment of RA 12326, however, Comelec stopped activities related to the November 2026 BSKE, including the filing of certificates of candidacy that had been scheduled for September 28 to October 5.
Garcia said the poll body's preparations would not necessarily go to waste, as election equipment already purchased can still be used for future elections. — VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Zelensky says Russia has widened attacks to hit Ukraine's data centres
articles.summary: Such strikes aim to disrupt "people's ability to stay connected, study, work", says Ukraine's president.

blocks.text: President Volodymyr Zelensky says Russia has widened its attacks to target Ukraine's data centres and internet providers, seeking to cause maximum disruption for ordinary people.
"All this affects people's ability to stay connected, study, work," he said.

On Friday a Russian drone hit a business centre in the capital Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. A separate attack killed a 14-year-old boy. Israel's foreign ministry said the teenager was an Israeli citizen.
Russia confirmed it had targeted a data centre site, saying it was being used by Ukrainian military intelligence.
About 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages on Wednesday due to strikes. Some firms are already transferring data from damaged servers abroad.

In the north-western city Lutsk, electronic information boards at public transport stops were not working on Friday, officials said. The city council said this was "due to damage caused by a Russian attack on data centres in Kyiv".

In a post on social media on Friday, Zelensky wrote: "The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centres, internet providers - for Russia, all ordinary life is simply a target.
"It is important that the world responds to all of this and that Russia feels the response to its terror."
On Wednesday, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russia was seeking to disrupt the flow of "life-saving information" by targeting data centres.

"Rapid alerts about missile and drone threats are essential - they save lives. This is critical civilian infrastructure... It is not a military target. It is essential to keeping everyday life functioning," Sybiha said.

Zelensky's top adviser on defence technologies on Thursday admitted that "there may be local disruptions" following Russian attacks an the cost of internet services could increase to cover the costs of repairs.
But Serhii Beskrestnov stressed that Ukraine's internet network was highly decentralised, so the country "will not be left without internet access".

The latest data centre hit by Russia is run by Datagroup. The company said its specialists were assessing the damage after Friday's daytime attack but all services "continue to operate from backup sites".
Russia's defence ministry later confirmed it had hit the Datagroup site, which it said was being used by the Ukrainian military's intelligence.
Footage showing the damaged Inkom business centre that housed Datagroup has since been verified by the BBC.

The Russian defence ministry also said that over the past few days its forces have targeted a number of data processing and telecommunications centres in Ukraine, including New-Telco, United DC, Kyivstar and Parkovyi.
In recent weeks, Moscow has also intensified its strikes on Ukraine's energy and railway infrastructure - seeking to cause maximum damage as winter approaches.
Ukraine's military has been hitting Russian oil refineries and logistics hubs, saying they help finance Russia's ongoing war effort.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In a separate development on Friday, Poland's prosecutors opened an investigation in what they said was an arson attack on a Starlink satellite station in Wola Krobowska on Wednesday.
In a statement, the national prosecutor's office said "there is a reasonable suspicion... that the perpetrators acted on the orders of the Russian special services". Moscow has not commented.
The station transmits internet traffic through Poland to countries including Ukraine, and uses SpaceX systems that provide connectivity via Starlink terminals.
In recent weeks a number of European Nato members have warned Russia may be preparing hybrid attacks to test their commitment to supporting Ukraine, which Moscow denies.
Earlier this month, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport, while France has ordered a plan to protect critical infrastructure and defence industry sites.

articles.title: Two arrested after people seen mysteriously emerging from various New York City sewers
articles.summary: The city has seen a string of incidents in which people have climbed out of manholes late at night.

blocks.text: New York officials arrested two of three men who they said were seen emerging from a manhole, exiting the city's underground sewer system on Wednesday.
The New York Police Department (NYPD) arrested 26-year-old Kevin Rodriguez and 25-year-old Samuel Reveron on charges of conspiracy and trespassing.
Three men were seen exiting a manhole near the hotel where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was reportedly expected to stay for the United Nations General Assembly.
In a statement to the BBC, the NYPD said it had seen a number of incidents involving people going into the sewer system to look for valuables and scrap metal after a storm.

"This incident fits that same criteria, but out of an abundance of caution given the U.N. General Assembly and the sensitivity of the location, the NYPD is conducting additional security sweeps with our federal partners," the police department said in a statement.

Rodriguez and Reveron, both from Queens, were arrested on Thursday. They allegedly fled the scene after climbing out of the manhole when officers were called around 4:30 EST (9:30 BST) on Wednesday, police said.
During a hearing on Friday morning, the two men pleaded not guilty and were released from custody, according to court records.
The arrests follow a string of incidents in which people were seen emerging from pavement manholes in different parts of the city in recent months.

In August, surveillance footage showed a person coming out of a manhole in Queens early in the morning. The same month, the NYPD said it was investigating three people wearing overalls and headlamps seen climbing out of a manhole near Penn Station.
In May, a group of people were captured on surveillance footage shifting a manhole cover and climbing down into the sewer in South Brooklyn.
Going into the New York sewer system is both illegal and dangerous, officials have said, cautioning that there is a risk of toxic gases and flooding in a confined space.
"For these reasons, members of the public should never enter a pipe, drain, catch basin, manhole, or outfall," the city's Department of Environmental Protection previously told the BBC.
This year, a woman died after she opened her car door and accidentally fell into an open manhole in Midtown Manhattan.
